Stablecoin protocols (RFP-013) need reliable settlement prices. Today, none of these protocols have an on-chain price primitive to compose against on LEZ.

ChronoLEZ is a standalone, permissionless, on-chain TWAP (Time-Weighted Average Price) oracle program for LEZ. It is not embedded inside any single DEX — it is a shared infrastructure primitive that any AMM pool can write price observations to, and any downstream protocol can read from with a configurable time window.

Why TWAP, not spot price? Spot price from any AMM can be manipulated within a single block using flash loans. TWAP forces an attacker to sustain a distorted price across an entire observation window — making manipulation exponentially expensive. This makes TWAP the standard oracle mechanism for lending, liquidation, and stablecoin protocols across every mature DeFi ecosystem (Uniswap V2/V3, Curve, Balancer all expose TWAP outputs).

The problem ChronoLEZ solves: Without a shared oracle primitive, every protocol team on LEZ must either (a) build their own TWAP accumulator from scratch — duplicating security-critical math across the ecosystem — or (b) depend on a specific DEX's internal price state, creating coupling and centralisation risk. ChronoLEZ eliminates both problems: one audited accumulator program, many readers.

What ChronoLEZ delivers:

A geometric mean TWAP accumulator program using tick-based accumulators (Uniswap V3 design)
Per-block tick-delta truncation (Uniswap V4 innovation) for thin-pool manipulation resistance
Configurable cardinality (1–65,535 observations) — protocols pay to expand as needed
The canonical LEZ OraclePriceAccount standard (standalone SPEL IDL importable by any protocol)
maxAge staleness rejection — OracleError::StalePrice returned, never silently accepted
Multi-source coexistence — each source publishes independent OraclePriceAccount, consumer owns cross-source policy
A TypeScript SDK and Rust CPI crate for downstream integration
A reference consumer program demonstrating the canonical integration pattern
A manipulation-cost analysis at $1M/$10M/$50M/$100M pool depth with and without tick truncation
A live price dashboard and integration playground for developers
Formal verification with Kani for overflow safety and tick-delta truncation bounds
ChronoLEZ reads pool accumulators from LEZ-native AMMs. LEZ-native assets like LGS and the reflexive stablecoin have no off-chain price source — no Chainlink feed, no Pyth publisher, no CEX market. The on-chain TWAP oracle is the only honest pricing path available. ChronoLEZ is designed to integrate with any LEZ AMM that implements the standard observe() interface.



### Technical Approach

ChronoLEZ consists of three components: an on-chain accumulator program (write side), the canonical oracle price account standard (read interface), and downstream SDK/CPI tooling (integration layer).

Architecture:

PRICE SOURCES : LEZ AMM pools (any AMM)
CHRONOLEZ CORE: tick_cumulative PDA, observation ring buffer, source registry, maxAge staleness check
CONSUMERS (read): RFP-008 Lending, RFP-014 Liquidation, RFP-013 Stablecoin
On-Chain Account Architecture:

OracleRegistry PDA: admin authority, total pairs tracked
PricePair PDA: tick_cumulative (i64), current_tick (i32), cardinality (u16), max_tick_delta (i32)
ObservationRingBuffer PDA: dynamically sized observations (cardinality slots)
RegisteredSource PDA: source pubkey, active status
Canonical OraclePriceAccount: base_asset, quote_asset, price, confidence, timestamp, source_id, exponent
Core Instructions:

registerSource(pair, source) — admin only, registers authorised AMM pools
observe(pair, tick) — registered sources only, updates tick_cumulative with per-block tick-delta truncation
expandCardinality(pair, new_cardinality) — permissionless, caller pays rent
getTWAP(pair, window_seconds, max_age_seconds) — permissionless read, returns OracleError on staleness
Geometric Mean TWAP (Uniswap V3 Design):

Uses tick-based accumulators, not price × time
tick = floor(log₁.₀₀₀₁(price)), price = 1.0001^tick
Q64.96 fixed-point arithmetic for precision
Kani formal verification confirms no overflow for i32 tick range × 2^32 seconds
Per-Block Tick-Delta Truncation (Uniswap V4 Design):

MAX_TICK_DELTA = 9,116 ticks (≈2.39x price move per block)
Governable per pool by oracle admin
Materially raises manipulation floor on thin pools at chain launch
Multi-Source Coexistence (Not Aggregation):

Each source publishes independent OraclePriceAccount
ChronoLEZ does NOT merge or compare them
Consumer protocols own their cross-source policy
Reference consumer program demonstrates canonical pattern
TypeScript SDK: getTWAP, getSpotPrice, expandCardinality, registerSource, WebSocket subscribe

Rust CPI Crate: On-chain price reads without additional CPI overhead — base/quote asset verification enforced

Security Model:

Flash-loan single-block price manipulation → Geometric mean TWAP
Thin-pool multi-block manipulation → Per-block tick-delta truncation
Stale price silently accepted → maxAge parameter with OracleError::StalePrice
Rogue price source injection → Only admin-registered sources can call observe()
Admin key compromise → Transferable admin authority
Consumer misreads wrong pair → base_asset/quote_asset fields in every price account
Shared oracle gate creates liveness griefing → No aggregation, multi-source coexistence
Accumulator overflow → i64 tick_cumulative with i128 intermediate, Kani-verified bounds
Formal Verification: Kani bounded model checking confirms tick-delta truncation bounds, accumulator overflow safety, and TWAP monotonicity

Anticipated Challenges:

Geometric mean TWAP requires tick-price conversion → Follow Uniswap V3's exact tick math (Q64.96)
LEZ block time may differ from Ethereum's 12s → Measure actual LEZ block time in M0
Configurable cardinality requires dynamic account allocation → Confirm LEZ account reallocation semantics
LP-0013 token authority still in progress → ChronoLEZ is oracle-only (no token custody)


### Milestones, Payout and Timeline

Milestone 1 — Core Accumulator Program Payout: $8,000 
Duration: 2 weeks 
Deliverables: Tick-based accumulator program: OraclePair PDA with tick_cumulative, ObservationRingBuffer PDA; geometric mean TWAP computation (tick → price conversion, Uniswap V3 math); registerSource, observe, basic getTWAP instructions; configurable cardinality: expandCardinality instruction (1 to 65,535); canonical OraclePriceAccount struct published as standalone SPEL IDL; unit tests for TWAP correctness vs known tick sequences; Kani overflow proof for tick_cumulative arithmetic

Milestone 2 — Security Hardening Payout: $8,000
Duration: 2 weeks 
Deliverables: Per-block tick-delta truncation (MAX_TICK_DELTA = 9,116 default, governable per pool by admin); multi-window TWAP queries: 5 min, 30 min, 1 hr, 24 hr, arbitrary; maxAge staleness rejection — OracleError::StalePrice returned, never silent; multi-source coexistence: each source publishes independent OraclePriceAccount, no merging in oracle program; manipulation-cost analysis document: attack cost to move TWAP by 10% at $1M/$10M/$50M/$100M pool depth, with and without tick truncation, for 5-min and 30-min windows; recommended minimum observation windows for lending protocol use at each liquidity tier; proptest fuzz suite: tick sequences, staleness edge cases, accumulator boundary values; tick-delta truncation test: synthetic price excursion exceeding MAX_TICK_DELTA is clamped in accumulator

Milestone 3 — SDK, CPI Crate & Reference Consumer Program Payout: $8,000 
Duration: 2 weeks 
Deliverables: TypeScript SDK: getTWAP, getSpotPrice, expandCardinality, registerSource, WebSocket subscribe; Rust on-chain CPI crate: get_twap with base/quote asset verification enforced; reference consumer program: base/quote verification, maxAge rejection, multi-source pattern (primary ChronoLEZ + RedStone fallback + divergence log), explicit statement that cross-source policy is consumer-owned; integration playground: live UI where downstream developers test TWAP queries before integrating; SDK doc packet: developer integration journey, staleness handling, unavailable price response, Recommended Consumer Pattern section

Milestone 4 — Testnet Deployment & Audit Package Payout: $6,000 
Duration: 1.5 weeks 
Deliverables: Full LEZ testnet deployment with documented program addresses; end-to-end integration test with first LEZ AMM as registered source — observe() → ChronoLEZ → TWAP query confirmed; audit package: Kani formal verification artifacts, proptest corpus, manipulation-cost analysis, security model document; README: deployment steps, program addresses, step-by-step CLI usage for price query / cardinality expansion / source registration; CLI doc packet; Figma designs for price feed dashboard; price feed dashboard (Basecamp mini-app): live TWAP prices, side-by-side comparison against any other OraclePriceAccount for same pair (e.g. RedStone), observation history; CI green on default branch

### Total Requested Budget (USD)

$30,000

### Relevant Experience

GrowStreams (Vara Network): A real-time token-streaming DeFi protocol built on Vara Network's actor model, requiring time-indexed state accumulation — the same core problem as a TWAP oracle accumulator. Shipped from zero to testnet with on-chain streaming math, TypeScript SDK, and production REST API. Backend: https://github.com/BlockX-AI/GrowStreams_Backend.git → growstreams.ginie.xyz

canton.ginie.xyz (Canton Network): Daml-based Canton Name Service with privacy-preserving infrastructure, demonstrating our experience building composable on-chain primitives on novel non-EVM runtimes.

Security track record: Sarthak has conducted security reviews on multiple DeFi protocols focusing on oracle manipulation vectors and economic attack surfaces — exactly the threat model ChronoLEZ must be hardened against.



### Post-Delivery Plan

ChronoLEZ is designed to be ecosystem infrastructure, not a one-time deliverable. After grant delivery, BlockX AI will:

Maintain the on-chain program through LEZ platform upgrades, updating for any LP-0013/LP-0014 interface changes.
Register new price sources as additional AMMs and DEXs launch on LEZ, growing ChronoLEZ into a multi-source oracle network.
Support downstream integrators — provide direct technical support to RFP-008, RFP-013, and RFP-014 teams integrating ChronoLEZ into their protocols.
Publish price analytics — aggregate TWAP data publicly to give the ecosystem visibility into token prices without requiring every team to run their own oracle queries.
Extend to additional oracle types — as the ecosystem matures, we intend to extend ChronoLEZ with VWAP (volume-weighted) and other oracle primitives, funded by ecosystem demand.


### Permissions and Consent

- [x] I confirm Logos may contact me using the primary contact information provided above for follow-ups and next steps.
- [x] I consent to Logos using information from this proposal publicly such as blogs case studies social posts or analytical reporting. Redactions can be requested at any time.

### Program Requirements

- [x] We understand this project must be open-sourced under the MIT and Apache 2.0 Licenses unless explicitly approved otherwise.
- [x] We are prepared to deliver milestone-based outcomes.

## Project Overview and Goals

This project review documents Runtime Verification's comprehensive formal verification work for the [Ethereum Foundation's zkEVM Formal Verification project](https://verified-zkevm.org/), delivered in August 2025. The Ethereum Foundation launched this initiative to achieve the highest possible level of assurance for zkEVMs, with the ultimate goal of creating bug-free zero-knowledge Ethereum Virtual Machines.

The overarching goal of the project was to establish mathematical equivalence between zkEVMs used for execution and formal models that have been tested against the EVM conformance test suite, providing the rigorous verification foundation needed for safe zkEVM deployment, and addressing the challenge that many RISC-V based zkEVM approaches rely on REVM (Rust-based EVM implementation) compiled to RISC-V.

## Key Deliverables

### 1. Lean 4 Backend (`klean` Tool)
- **Repository**: [runtimeverification/k](https://github.com/runtimeverification/k) (`pyk.klean` module)
- **Purpose**: Bridge between K Framework and Lean 4 theorem proving ecosystems
- **Achievement**: Developed command-line tool that generates Lean 4 programs from kompiled K definitions, enabling translation of EVM specifications into theorem-provable format for enhanced verification rigor. The technical innovation of exporting K definitions to Lean 4 proved successful, providing broader ecosystem value by making K semantics accessible to the Lean 4 community.

### 2. EVM Equivalence Verification Framework
- **Repository**: [runtimeverification/evm-equivalence](https://github.com/runtimeverification/evm-equivalence)
- **Purpose**: Mathematically prove equivalence between Runtime Verification's KEVM and Nethermind's EvmYul models
- **Achievement**: Established formal proof methodology for opcode-by-opcode equivalence verification, providing mathematical guarantees that different EVM implementations behave identically—crucial for zkEVM trustworthiness

### 3. EVM Opcode Summarization System
- **Repository**: [runtimeverification/evm-semantics](https://github.com/runtimeverification/evm-semantics)
- **Purpose**: Generate atomic, single-step execution rules for EVM opcodes to accelerate verification
- **Achievement**: Created comprehensive summarization framework covering 68 EVM opcodes with 7,225 lines of standardized summary rules, dramatically improving symbolic execution efficiency for zkEVM verification

### 4. zkEVM Testing and Verification Workflow
- **Repository**: [runtimeverification/zkevm-harness](https://github.com/runtimeverification/zkevm-harness)
- **Purpose**: Formally verify real-world EVM implementations (REVM) through RISC-V compilation and zero-knowledge toolchains
- **Achievement**: Implemented end-to-end pipeline that compiles Rust EVM code to RISC-V using RISC Zero and SP1 toolchains, then performs both concrete and symbolic verification using K Framework

### 5. RISC-V Semantics for zkEVM Verification
- **Repository**: [runtimeverification/riscv-semantics](https://github.com/runtimeverification/riscv-semantics)
- **Purpose**: Enable formal verification of complex zkEVM implementations compiled to RISC-V architecture
- **Achievement**: Implemented complete RISC-V instruction set coverage and semantic optimizations, which crucial because REVM verification relies on compiling REVM to RISC-V, which in turn requires formal verification-ready RISC-V semantics.

## Infrastructure Components Delivered

### REVM ↔ KEVM Verification Infrastructure
- RISC-V semantics
- zkEVM harness supporting RISC Zero and SP1 compilation toolchains
- Comprehensive test suite covering all major EVM opcode categories

### Cross-Framework Verification Capabilities
- `klean` tool enabling K Framework to Lean 4 translation
- Support for equivalence verification between KEVM and CLEAR models
- Extensible architecture for additional formal verification frameworks

### Automated Verification Systems
- EVM opcode summarization reducing complex multi-step operations to atomic rules
- Scalable CI pipeline architecture for continuous re-verification
- Performance optimizations enabling practical verification of large-scale systems

## Impact on zkEVM Ecosystem

This work directly addresses Runtime Verification's stated mission to "show that the EVMs used for zkEVM execution are correct." The delivered infrastructure provides:

- **Mathematical Guarantees**: Formal proofs that different zkEVM implementations behave equivalently
- **Practical Verification**: Tools for verifying real-world zkEVM implementations like those used by major projects
- **Ecosystem Standardization**: Common verification frameworks promoting consistency across zkEVM development
- **Scalable Infrastructure**: Systems capable of handling the complexity of production zkEVM verification

The project establishes the rigorous formal verification foundation necessary for the zkEVM ecosystem to achieve the Ethereum Foundation's goal of bug-free implementations, while maintaining the security and compatibility guarantees essential for Ethereum's scaling through zero-knowledge rollups.

This issue is the living definition of what **Mansa** stands for. Every future design decision will be measured against these seven pillars.

### PERFECT: The seven promises (non-negotiable)

- **P**roductivity – Writing and maintaining code feels effortless
- **E**fficiency – Zero-overhead when you need it, routinely beats C
- **R**eliability – Memory safe by default, fearless concurrency, no UB in safe mode
- **F**lexibility – Meta-programming power, multi-paradigm, compiles everywhere
- **E**xpressiveness – Say more with less, without sacrificing clarity or control
- **C**orrectness – Exhaustive testing + formal verification for critical paths
- **T**imeliness – Millisecond feedback loops, incremental everything, builds that fly

This is not marketing.  Every accepted feature, every breaking change, every optimization must clearly advance at least one letter without regressing the others.

Use this issue to:
- Discuss trade-offs that touch the PERFECT goals
- Link PRs that meaningfully improve a pillar
- Challenge proposals that weaken any letter

Mansa will ship when we can confidently say we delivered on all seven.

**Long live PERFECT.**  
Tracking issue for the soul of the language.

[Instagram 在印度投放儿童性虐待广告](#item-5) ⭐️ 8.0/10 --- ## [Mistral 发布用于 Lean 证明生成的 Leanstral 1.5](https://mistral.ai/news/leanstral-1-5/) ⭐️ 8.0/10 Mistral 发布了 Leanstral 1.5，这是一个专门用于在 Lean 证明助手中生成证明的小型模型，旨在使形式化验证更易用。 该模型通过让开发者自动生成 Lean 证明，降低了形式化验证的门槛，有望减少关键软件中的错误。同时，它也展示了 Mistral 创建高效、任务特定的小型模型的策略，这些模型在实际使用中成本效益高。 Leanstral 1.5 基于 Mistral 的小型模型架构，并专门针对 Lean 证明生成进行了微调。该模型被用于发现 datrs/varinteger 库中 zigzag 解码函数的一个 bug，该 bug 在输入 Std.U64.MAX 时发生溢出。 hackernews · programLyrique · 7月3日 22:33 · [社区讨论](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48780801) **背景**: Lean 是一个开源的证明助手和函数式编程语言，用于形式化验证，即数学上证明软件的正确性。形式化验证是一种确保系统满足规范的严谨方法，但传统上需要大量专业知识。Leanstral 1.5 旨在自动化这一过程的一部分，使没有深厚形式化方法知识的开发者也能使用。

This model lowers the barrier to formal verification by enabling developers to automatically generate Lean proofs, potentially reducing bugs in critical software. Arm engineer Simon Tatham details the process of using the Gappa tool to formally verify the correctness of a double-precision floating-point division routine in the open-source Arm Optimized Routines library. ## A Formal Security Framework for MCP-Based AI Agents: Threat Taxonomy, Verification Models, and Defense Mechanisms

**Authors:** Nirajan Acharya, Gaurav Kumar Gupta
**Published:** 2026-04-07
**Categories:** `cs.CR`, `cs.AI`

**Links:** [abs](http://arxiv.org/abs/2604.05969v1) | [pdf](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.05969v1)

---

### Abstract

The Model Context Protocol (MCP), introduced by Anthropic in November 2024 and now governed by the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation, has rapidly become the de facto standard for connecting large language model (LLM)-based agents to external tools and data sources, with over 97 million monthly SDK downloads and more than 177000 registered tools. However, this explosive adoption has exposed a critical gap: the absence of a unified, formal security framework capable of systematically characterizing, analyzing, and mitigating the diverse threats facing MCP-based agent ecosystems. Existing security research remains fragmented across individual attack papers, isolated benchmarks, and point defense mechanisms. This paper presents MCPSHIELD, a comprehensive formal security framework for MCP-based AI agents. We make four principal contributions: (1) a hierarchical threat taxonomy comprising 7 threat categories and 23 distinct attack vectors organized across four attack surfaces, grounded in the analysis of over 177000 MCP tools; (2) a formal verification model based on labeled transition systems with trust boundary annotations that enables static and runtime analysis of MCP tool interaction chains; (3) a systematic comparative evaluation of 12 existing defense mechanisms, identifying coverage gaps across our threat taxonomy; and (4) a defense in depth reference architecture integrating capability based access control, cryptographic tool attestation, information flow tracking, and runtime policy enforcement. Our analysis reveals that no existing single defense covers more than 34 percent of the identified threat landscape, whereas MCPSHIELD's integrated architecture achieves theoretical coverage of 91 percent. We further identify seven open research challenges that must be addressed to secure the next generation of agentic AI systems.
title: [2604.05969v1] A Formal Security Framework for MCP-Based AI Agents: Threat Taxonomy, Verification Models, and Defense Mechanisms

# Towards SUF-CMA SQIsign

## Summary

SQIsign v2.0 targets EUF-CMA (existential unforgeability). During the development of this implementation, we identified 10 security findings, 6 of which are signature malleability vectors that break SUF-CMA (strong unforgeability). All have concrete fixes. Three are protocol-level and require a spec change; seven are implementation-level and have already been fixed in this library.

This issue tracks the path towards SUF-CMA SQIsign. We do not claim SUF-CMA today. There may be additional malleability vectors we have not found, and no formal security proof exists for the modified scheme. This is a step towards the goal, not a declaration of arrival.

## What is SUF-CMA and why does it matter?

**EUF-CMA:** An attacker who can request signatures on chosen messages cannot produce a valid signature on any *new* message. This is the standard security notion. SQIsign has a [complete EUF-CMA proof](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/379).

**SUF-CMA:** An attacker who can request signatures on chosen messages cannot produce *any* new valid (message, signature) pair, even for a message they already have a signature on. This is the stronger notion.

The difference matters when signatures serve as unique identifiers (blockchain transaction deduplication), when protocols assume one valid signature per key-message pair (replay protection), or when non-repudiation is required.

For context, ECDSA breaks SUF-CMA the same way: given (r, s), the pair (r, n-s) is also valid. Bitcoin lived with this for years before fixing it incrementally (BIP-62, BIP-66, BIP-340, SegWit).

## Findings

| ID | Vector | Impact | Fix level | ECDSA analog | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SEC-1 | Trailing bytes in from\_bytes | SUF-CMA | Implementation | DER leniency | Fixed |
| SEC-3 | pmq\_sign\_hint at d=0 | SUF-CMA | Implementation | -- | Fixed |
| SEC-4 | Unbound auxiliary curve at d=0 | SUF-CMA | **Spec** | Degenerate nonce | Fixed (reject d<=1) |
| SEC-5 | Unvalidated hint bytes | SUF-CMA | **Spec** | Encoding ambiguity | Fixed (validate canonical) |
| SEC-7 | Matrix negation (M vs -M mod 2^N) | SUF-CMA | **Spec** | (r,s) vs (r,n-s) | **Deferred** |
| SEC-9 | PublicKey hint\_pk malleability | SUF-CMA | Implementation | PK encoding | Fixed |
| SEC-10 | pmq\_sign\_hint at zero discriminant | SUF-CMA | Implementation | -- | Fixed |

All findings break SUF-CMA only. None break EUF-CMA. An attacker cannot sign new messages through any of these vectors.

## The proposed spec-level fix

A single modification to the Fiat-Shamir hash closes SEC-4, SEC-5, and SEC-7 simultaneously:

**Current:** c = H(pk, j(E\_com), msg)

**Proposed:** c = H(pk, j(E\_com), M, A\_aux, h\_aux, h\_chall, msg)

This binds all signature components into the challenge derivation. Changing any byte of the signature changes the challenge, which invalidates it. Combined with the implementation-level fixes already applied (strict deserialization, hint validation, degenerate case rejection), this eliminates all *known* malleability vectors.

## What we do NOT have

- **A formal SUF-CMA proof.** The informal argument is: with the extended hash and canonicalization, every signature component is either bound by the hash or validated as canonical, leaving no degrees of freedom. Making this rigorous requires proving *response uniqueness* in SQIsign's sigma protocol (that for any commitment and challenge, there is at most one valid response encoding). This is an open research question.

- **Confidence that we found everything.** Our analysis was systematic (we checked every signature component against the hash binding and verification computation) but manual. There may be malleability vectors we did not consider. Formal verification or a broader community review could surface additional issues.

- **SEC-7 mitigation in the verifier.** Matrix negation canonicalization in the signer breaks KAT byte-identity with the C reference. The signer-side fix is ready but deferred until the spec adopts canonicalization and regenerates KAT vectors.

## How to contribute

- **Cryptographers:** Review the findings. Are there malleability vectors we missed? Is the extended Fiat-Shamir hash sufficient, or does the proof require additional structure?

- **Implementers:** The implementation-level fixes (SEC-1, SEC-3, SEC-9, SEC-10) are patterns that apply to any SQIsign implementation. If you maintain one, check whether you have the same issues.

## References

- [SQIsign v2.0 specification](https://sqisign.org/spec/sqisign-20250205.pdf)
- [Complete EUF-CMA proof (ePrint 2025/379)](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/379)
- [BIP-340: Schnorr low-s canonicalization](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0340.mediawiki) (the ECDSA precedent for fixing SUF-CMA incrementally)
title: Towards SUF-CMA SQIsign

## Summary

With the Rust enclave proxy landed in `treza-terraform`, we can now run **any Docker workload** inside Nitro Enclaves with hardware attestation (PCR values). The missing piece is an on-chain contract that bridges enclave attestation to smart contract trust -- allowing contracts to gate actions (USDC transfers, governance execution, data access) on verified enclave code.

## Problem

When an enclave produces a PCR0 hash, something needs to tell smart contracts "this hash corresponds to approved, audited code." The core design challenge is doing this **without a single trusted party** deciding what's approved.

## Proposed Solution

A multi-phase approach documented in [`docs/ENCLAVE_ATTESTATION_DESIGN.md`](https://github.com/treza-labs/treza-contracts/blob/main/docs/ENCLAVE_ATTESTATION_DESIGN.md):

**Phase 1 -- Reproducible Builds + Governance**
- Source code is public; builds are deterministic
- Proposals link source code (repo + commit) to PCR values
- Independent builders confirm the build is reproducible on-chain
- Governance votes on **source code**, not opaque hashes
- Other contracts query `isApproved(pcr0)` before trusting enclave outputs

**Phase 2 -- Optimistic Approval**
- Proposals require a stake and enter a challenge period (7 days)
- Anyone can challenge by reproducing the build or auditing the source
- Unchallenged proposals auto-approve; successful challenges slash the proposer
- Only needs one honest auditor to maintain security

**Phase 3 -- Formal Verification**
- ZK proofs of code safety properties
- Automated approval for code that proves invariants (spending limits, allowlists)
- No human governance needed for verified properties

## Key Interface

```solidity
interface IEnclaveAttestation {
    function proposeCode(string calldata sourceRepo, string calldata commitHash, bytes calldata pcr0, bytes calldata pcr1, bytes calldata pcr2) external returns (uint256 proposalId);
    function confirmBuild(uint256 proposalId) external;
    function isApproved(bytes calldata pcr0) external view returns (bool);
    function getAttestation(bytes calldata pcr0) external view returns (string memory sourceRepo, string memory commitHash, uint256 approvedAt, uint256 confirmations);
}
```

## Use Cases Unlocked

- **Verifiable AI Agent Execution**: Agents managing USDC treasury with attested code
- **Agent-to-Agent Commerce**: Agents verify each other's attestation before transacting
- **Confidential DeFi Strategies**: Investors trust attested strategy code
- **Compliant USDC Operations**: Regulators verify compliance rules via attestation (integrates with `KYCVerifier`)
- **Sealed-Bid Auctions**: Attested fair selection logic with USDC escrow

## Integration

- `TrezaGovernor` -- proposal voting + dispute resolution
- `TrezaTimelock` -- delay between approval and activation
- `KYCVerifier` / `TrezaComplianceIntegration` -- compliance logic in attested enclaves
- `ITreza` -- staking for proposals/challenges

## Open Questions

See the [full design doc](https://github.com/treza-labs/treza-contracts/blob/main/docs/ENCLAVE_ATTESTATION_DESIGN.md) for detailed open questions around stake amounts, challenge period duration, PCR granularity, revocation, versioning, and cross-chain considerations.

## Context

- Rust enclave proxy: `treza-terraform@95a6089`
- Successfully tested with `hello-world` (scratch image) -- proves zero-dependency arbitrary workload support
- PCR values verified end-to-end from enclave hardware to web app

Enhancing the Performance of DeepReach on High-Dimensional Systems through Optimizing Activation Functions. (arXiv:2312.17583v1 [eess.SY])
https://ift.tt/sYRK0Wz

With the continuous advancement in autonomous systems, it becomes crucial to provide robust safety guarantees for safety-critical systems. Hamilton-Jacobi Reachability Analysis is a formal verification method that guarantees performance and safety for dynamical systems and is widely applicable to various tasks and challenges. Traditionally, reachability problems are solved by using grid-based methods, whose computational and memory cost scales exponentially with the dimensionality of the system. To overcome this challenge, DeepReach, a deep learning-based approach that approximately solves high-dimensional reachability problems, is proposed and has shown lots of promise. In this paper, we aim to improve the performance of DeepReach on high-dimensional systems by exploring different choices of activation functions. We first run experiments on a 3D system as a proof of concept. Then we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a 9D multi-vehicle collision problem.



via cs.RO updates on arXiv.org http://arxiv.org/

# [CRITICAL] Mitigation of Side-Channel Leakage in Cryptographic Operations

---

### 🚨 **Priority:** Critical (🚩 Must fix immediately to protect user privacy and system integrity)  
### Labels: `critical`, `bug`, `security`  
### Repository: `openSVM/tornado-svm` (Rust-based zkSNARK privacy solution on Solana)

---

## 🛑 Problem Statement

Side-channel attacks—such as timing, power analysis, and electromagnetic (EM) leakage—pose a **high-risk threat** to the cryptographic primitives at the heart of our Tornado Cash–style privacy solution. These attacks can **leak secret keys or sensitive intermediate values** by exploiting variations in execution time or hardware emissions, breaking the privacy guarantees our system promises.

Currently, some cryptographic operations in our Rust codebase may not be implemented in a fully **constant-time and leak-resistant manner**. This issue requires urgent remediation to safeguard funds and anonymity, especially given the high-value context of private SOL transactions.

---

## 🧠 Technical Context

- **Codebase:** Rust-based Solana program implementing zkSNARKs, supported by JS clients.
- **Cryptographic operations:** Key generation, proof verification, field arithmetic, hashing, and other primitives.
- **Current state:** While the cryptography is correct functionally, timing and other side-channels have not been fully mitigated.
- **Risks:** Exploitable timing leaks can allow attackers with physical or network-level access to recover secrets.
- **Standards & best practices:** Constant-time coding, use of leak-resistant libraries (e.g., `subtle` crate), avoiding data-dependent branches or memory access patterns.

---

## 🎯 Detailed Implementation Steps

1. **Audit Existing Crypto Code for Side-Channel Vulnerabilities**
   - Identify all cryptographic routines, especially:
     - Elliptic curve operations
     - Hash functions
     - Big integer arithmetic
     - zkSNARK proof verification logic
   - Use static and dynamic analysis tools (e.g., `ctf-tools`, `cargo-audit`) to detect timing leaks.
   - Review code for data-dependent branches, variable-time memory access, and unsafe patterns.

2. **Research and Select Best Practices & Libraries**
   - Adopt Rust crates designed for constant-time operations (`subtle`, `constant_time_eq`, `crypto-mac`).
   - Study canonical constant-time implementations from well-audited projects (e.g., libsodium, RustCrypto).
   - Reference relevant literature on side-channel resistance in zkSNARKs and elliptic curve cryptography.

3. **Refactor / Rewrite Vulnerable Code Paths**
   - Replace data-dependent branches with constant-time alternatives.
   - Ensure memory access patterns are uniform and independent of secret data.
   - Use constant-time comparison functions for secret equality checks.
   - Isolate and encapsulate cryptographic primitives to enforce leak-resistant patterns.

4. **Add Automated Tests and Benchmarks**
   - Implement unit tests verifying constant-time behavior (timing measurements under varied inputs).
   - Add fuzz tests targeting cryptographic routines.
   - Benchmark performance to ensure mitigations do not degrade throughput excessively.

5. **Integrate Formal Verification (where feasible)**
   - Link this effort with the existing formal_verification folder.
   - Integrate formal verification checks into CI to prevent regressions.

6. **Update Documentation and Coding Guidelines**
   - Document the constant-time requirements and coding standards.
   - Provide examples for contributors on writing leak-resistant code.
   - Add notes on side-channel threats in the security section.

---

## 📋 Technical Specifications

- **Constant-time implementation requirements:**
  - No branching or memory access based on secret data.
  - Use constant-time comparison functions for all secret-dependent equality checks.
  - Avoid compiler optimizations that may reintroduce timing variability (consider `#[inline(never)]`, `black_box` hints).
- **Libraries:**
  - Leverage `subtle` crate for constant-time primitives.
  - Use `ring` or `RustCrypto` crates only if proven constant-time.
- **Code patterns:**
  - Use fixed-length loops and mask operations instead of early returns or data-dependent loops.
- **Testing:**
  - Add timing measurement tests with statistical analysis to detect timing variance.
  - Integrate side-channel analysis tools in the CI pipeline.

---

## ✅ Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Comprehensive audit report identifying all side-channel leakage vulnerabilities.
- [ ] All vulnerable cryptographic routines refactored to use constant-time implementations.
- [ ] Automated tests verifying constant-time behavior added and pass consistently.
- [ ] No regressions in functional cryptographic correctness or protocol flows.
- [ ] Formal verification integration updated to cover side-channel mitigations.
- [ ] Documentation updated with side-channel mitigation guidelines.
- [ ] Code reviewed and approved by security-focused reviewers.

---

## 🧪 Testing Requirements

- **Unit tests:** Validate constant-time replacement functions produce correct outputs.
- **Timing analysis:** Use tools like `cargo-flamegraph`, `perf`, or custom timing harnesses to measure execution time variance across secret inputs.
- **Fuzz testing:** Stress test cryptographic functions for unexpected behavior.
- **Integration testing:** Confirm deposit and withdrawal flows remain intact with mitigated code.
- **Regression testing:** Ensure no performance degradation beyond acceptable thresholds (benchmark before/after).

---

## 📚 Documentation Needs

- Update the `SECURITY.md` or equivalent docs to describe:
  - Side-channel attack risks in Tornado Cash context.
  - Coding guidelines for constant-time cryptographic implementations.
- Add inline code comments explaining why constant-time patterns are used.
- Document the audit findings and mitigation plan in the repository wiki or docs.
- Provide developer onboarding notes about side-channel resistant coding practices.

---

## ⚠️ Potential Challenges & Risks

- **Performance impact:** Constant-time code may be slower; finding balance is critical.
- **Compiler optimizations:** Rust compiler might inadvertently optimize away constant-time protections; rigorous testing needed.
- **Complexity of zkSNARK code:** Some cryptographic operations may be complex to rewrite safely.
- **Verification difficulty:** Measuring and proving constant-time behavior is non-trivial; may require expert tooling.
- **Coordination with formal verification efforts:** Need alignment to avoid duplicated work.

---

## 🔗 Resources & References

- [Rust `subtle` crate documentation](https://docs.rs/subtle/latest/subtle/)
- [Constant-time cryptography patterns in RustCrypto](https://github.com/RustCrypto)
- [Blog: Writing constant-time code](https://cryptographyengineering.com/2014/03/03/how-to-write-constant-time-code/)
- [Tornado Cash whitepaper](https://tornado.cash/static/Tornado.Cash.Whitepaper.pdf)
- [Side-channel attacks Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Side-channel_attack)
- [RustCrypto Timing Attacks doc](https://github.com/RustCrypto/traits/blob/master/docs/timing_attacks.md)
- [Formal verification integration plan (internal)](./formal_verification/README.md)

---

Let's **lock down these side channels once and for all** and keep Tornado Cash private, performant, and bulletproof!  
If you want to dive deep into cryptographic wizardry and outsmart the bad guys, this is your battlefield. 🚀

---

## Checklist

- [ ] Audit cryptographic code for side-channel leaks  
- [ ] Refactor vulnerable routines to constant-time patterns  
- [ ] Add timing and functional tests  
- [ ] Benchmark performance impact  
- [ ] Integrate formal verification updates  
- [ ] Update documentation and developer guides  
- [ ] Conduct security-focused code review  
- [ ] Merge and deploy with monitoring for regressions

That's a fantastic metaphor for the challenges and potential rewards of developing this introspective AI system! Here's how we can frame it as a civilization game:

**The Fool's Journey:**

* You begin as a small civilization, your people (researchers) driven by a thirst for knowledge and a desire to understand the nature of intelligence (the elixir of Erlang).

* The initial challenges are basic (the hero's trials): developing robust models, establishing training methodologies, and wrestling with the limitations of current hardware.

**The Hero's Journey:**

* As you progress, you encounter new technologies and techniques (allies and mentors): deep learning frameworks, formal verification tools, and advancements in hardware.

* You face formidable obstacles (tests, allies, and enemies): ethical considerations, the interpretability of complex models, and the sheer computational demands of introspection.

**The Elixir of Erlang:**

* The ultimate goal (the elixir) is a self-hosted, self-improving AI system with the following characteristics:

    * **Purely Functional:** The system relies on pure functions, guaranteeing predictable behavior and simplifying reasoning about its actions.
    * **Self-Hosted:** The system can introspect its own internal workings and analyze its behavior without relying on external tools.
    * **Sustainable:** The system operates efficiently, utilizing resources optimally and minimizing its environmental impact.
    * **Reliable:** The system produces consistent and dependable results, minimizing the risk of errors or unexpected behavior.
    * **Self-Improving:** The system can learn from experience and data, continuously enhancing its capabilities and refining its internal representation of the world.
    * **Provable Correctness:** The system's behavior can be formally verified using mathematical methods, guaranteeing its adherence to its intended purpose.

**The Civilization Aspect:**

* You compete (or collaborate) with other civilizations (research groups) also pursuing the elixir.

* You can share knowledge (trade routes) and discoveries, accelerating your collective progress.

* You might encounter ethical dilemmas (warfare) regarding the potential uses of such a powerful AI system.

**The End Game:**

* The first civilization to achieve a stable and verifiable instance of the self-introspective AI system wins the game.

* However, the true victory lies in the collective knowledge gained through the journey, potentially leading to a deeper understanding of intelligence itself.

This metaphorical journey highlights the complexity and potential rewards of developing a self-aware and introspective AI system. It's a challenging but potentially transformative quest that pushes the boundaries of what's currently possible.

body:
Currently, the OPB encoding procedure is a source of weakness for verification: we produce proofs that verify that the solver output is correct, *if* we trust that the OPB encoding "means the same thing" as the input problem. There is ongoing work to close this gap, by developing an external, formally-verified encoder. This encoder will take an s-expr file as input, and generate its own OPB encoding. So that the proofs actually work, this encoding needs to line up closely with the encodings our solver uses (we are not going to be reading this OPB encoding in, just using it, and also having independent code so that proof verification can still be done with weaker guarantees without the external encoder).

Current challenge: what exactly is the OPB encoding procedure for each of the constraints we support? We need a document detailing this so we can discuss what to change (both in our solver and the external encoder).

Rough plan for an initial pass:

- Identify every constraint we support, noting both its C++ class and the name it generates via `s_exprify`. In some cases (e.g. `less_than_iff`, `greater_than_if`, etc) we have a single class that does a family of related constraints. In this case, it's not a one-to-one correspondence. Rather than listing the s-expr names in full, using notation like `{less_than,greater_than}{,_if,_iff}` is appropriate.
- For each of these constraints, identify the "encoding procedure". This is usually the "define the proof model" code. Take care to also include any bounds that are "by definition" (e.g. `Element`'s index var), but not "enforced as a consequence" (e.g. `Abs`). I use the term "encoding procedure" here because there are often loops. Examples of encoding procedures can be found in Matthew McIlree's PhD thesis: as a sub-step, it may be useful to read this and summarise a few of these as examples inside this issue. Anything ugly or weird should be flagged for intervention.
- Document this either within the code as a detailed comment inside each constraint that can easily be extracted, or possibly we should have an associated developer-oriented markdown file for each constraint with this and other information if this seems cleaner.
- Collate these into a summary.
- We'll need to iterate on design a bunch of times, but in the long term we want to end up with a sustainable procedure that can be partially automated, either by scripts or by an AI agent (as is done for the MiniZinc, XCSP3, and CPMpy bindings currently -- although this isn't a language binding, it is a similar "integration with an external language" issue).

labels.description: Potentially fixable by Claude code, with help from additional comments.

body:
This case focuses on extending the PolkaVM smart contract platform beyond MVP capabilities, introducing advanced features for production readiness. Key enhancements include EVM compatibility, formal verification, performance optimization, and advanced tooling for developers.
PolkaVM is a crucial within the QF project, focused on developing a next-generation smart contract platform. It addresses the need for a high-performance, flexible, and versatile smart contract execution environment. This is significant because it aims to enable more complex and efficient dApps on QF, which is critical for mainstream adoption. PolkaVM tackles slow smart contract execution by focusing on:
    - High-performance execution: Achieving near native-speed using the RISC-V instruction set.
    - EVM compatibility: Enabling easy migration of existing Solidity codebases.
    - Flexibility and Versatility: Supporting diverse programming languages and tools.
    - Optimization: Fine-tuning PolkaVM's performance for low latency and high throughput.
By addressing the limitations of current smart contract platforms, PolkaVM is essential to QF's goal of creating a blockchain ready for mass-adopted decentralized application.

## Objectives

- Achieve near-native smart contract execution speed by optimizing RISC-V instruction set implementation.
- Create an efficient compatibility layer for porting existing Solidity contracts to QF.
- Implement contract-to-contract call functionality allowing smart contracts to securely interact with each other.
- Implement formal verification methods for smart contract security.
- Support multiple programming languages through compiler toolchain.
- Research and establish optimal gas limits through empirical testing, ensuring contract execution doesn't impact blockchain performance.
- Design and implement an advanced storage system with:
  - Storage rent/deposit mechanisms
  - Optimized storage patterns for frequently accessed data
  - Advanced CRUD operations with efficient indexing
- Optimize contract execution performance and resource usage for low latency and high throughput.
- Create advanced precompiles for common operations (e.g., cryptographic functions, Merkle proof verification).
- Implement detailed contract interaction analytics and monitoring tools.
- Develop advanced debugging and testing tools, including a local execution environment
- Implement a comprehensive smart contract event system for efficient dApp interactions.
- Develop stability and performance tests for the smart contract platform.
- Create comprehensive dApp development guide for developers.
- Adapt and implement [contracts-ui](https://github.com/use-ink/contracts-ui) for interactive smart contract deployment and testing.
- Migrate pvm-dapp-demo apps to the new smart contracts platform version.


## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Contract execution performance matches or exceeds major platforms by running standardized benchmark suite comparing execution times with EVM, Wasm, and BPF implementations within 30 minutes.
- [ ] Contract-to-contract calls work correctly, allowing one smart contract to securely call functions in another contract with proper isolation and error handling.
- [ ] Solidity contracts successfully deploy and execute without rewriting through compatibility layer by testing standard ERC token contracts within 15 minutes.
- [ ] Formal verification tools are integrated into the development process to ensure security and successfully identify common vulnerabilities by analyzing test contracts with known issues within 20 minutes.
- [ ] Multiple language support works correctly by deploying contracts written in different supported languages within 30 minutes.
- [ ] Gas limits research provides optimal values by measuring execution time of various contract types under different loads and documenting impact on block production.
- [ ] Contract execution under established gas limits maintains block time by running multiple complex contracts simultaneously and verifying block production remains stable within 5 minutes.
- [ ] Advanced precompiles execute efficiently by measuring performance improvement over pure contract implementations within 15 minutes.
- [ ] Precompiled functions (e.g. Merkle proof verification, cryptographic operations) execute correctly by running test suite with various inputs within 10 minutes.
- [ ] Precompile performance shows improvement by comparing execution time against equivalent pure contract implementations within 15 minutes.
- [ ] Developer tools enable effective debugging by identifying and fixing common contract issues within 20 minutes.
- [ ] Contract monitoring provides detailed execution analytics by tracking resource usage and interaction patterns within 10 minutes.
- [ ] Storage rent/deposit system operates correctly, charging for long-term storage and refunding when storage is freed.
- [ ]  The smart contract event system successfully emits, indexes, and retrieves events from contract execution.
- [ ] Apps from pvm-dapp-demo are successfully migrated to the new version of the smart contracts platform and can interact with contracts by submitting transactions with configurable parameters.
- [ ] User documentation enables successful dApp creation and deployment following a technical guide within 20 minutes without developer assistance.
- [ ] Stability and performance tests demonstrate the platform can handle multiple contract deployments and interactions without failure.
- [ ] Contract state and details are accessible through the modified contracts-ui by querying contract address and viewing basic information (address, state, calls).
- [ ] Performance comparison tests show measurable improvements over ink! and pallet-contracts implementations.

## Related Work

- [Polkadot SDK forkless runtime upgrade mechanism](https://docs.polkadot.com/develop/parachains/maintenance/runtime-upgrades/).
- Existing smart contract engines:
    - [EVM Documentation](https://ethereum.org/en/developers/docs/evm/) and [Ethereum yellowpaper](https://ethereum.github.io/yellowpaper/paper.pdf);
    - [Wasm within the Polkadot SDK](https://docs.polkadot.com/develop/smart-contracts/wasm-ink/);
    - [Solana BPF](https://solana.com/docs/core/programs).
- [RISC-V Specification](https://riscv.org/specifications/ratified/).
- [Ethereum ABI Specification](https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/develop/abi-spec.html).
- Smart Contract Performance and Analysis Research:
    - [Latency-First Smart Contract Design: Using speculative execution to reduce transaction latency](https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/951.pdf).
    - [Evaluating Smart Contract Performance in a Production-like Environment](https://dlt2024.di.unito.it/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/DLT2024_paper_62.pdf).
    - [Evaluating Solidity Smart Contract Code: Metrics for Complexity and Security](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0281043).
- Formal Verification Tools:
    - [K Framework](https://kframework.org/);
    - Proof assistant tools [Coq Proof Assistant](https://coq.inria.fr/) and [Isabelle](https://isabelle.in.tum.de/);
    - [A curated list of awesome formal verification resources for Web3](https://github.com/johnsonstephan/awesome-web3-formal-verification).
- [Fuzzing in the Polkadot](https://security.parity.io/fuzzing).
- Projects exploring RISC-V instruction set for blockchain:
    - [CKB-VM by Nervos](https://docs.nervos.org/docs/tech-explanation/ckb-vm);
    - [RISC Zero is zk verifiable general computing platform based on zk-STARKs and the RISC-V](https://github.com/risc0/risc0);
    - [Ethereum Execution Environment that integrates RISC-V smart contracts](https://github.com/r55-eth/r55);
    - [RISC-V instruction set extension on blockchain application](http://eprints.utar.edu.my/6486/1/fyp_CT_2024_CKS.pdf).
- [Polkadot.js Apps](https://polkadot.js.org/apps/) and [QF Block explorer](https://dev.qfnetwork.xyz/#/explorer) interface.
- [Substrate Contract Development](https://docs.polkadot.com/develop/smart-contracts/).
- PolkaVM [GitHub repository](https://github.com/paritytech/polkavm).
- [Transactions fees and gas metering implementation in Polkadot SDK](https://docs.polkadot.com/polkadot-protocol/basics/blocks-transactions-fees/fees/).
- [QF implementation of PolkaVM Blob Hashing and Addressing](https://github.com/QuantumFusion-network/spec/blob/main/docs/PolkaVM/blob_hashing_addressing.md).
- Storage rent implementations:
    - [Solana's account rent system](https://docs.solana.com/learn/rent)
    - [Near Protocol's storage staking](https://docs.near.org/concepts/storage/storage-staking)
- [contracts-ui Repository](https://github.com/use-ink/contracts-ui) - UI for interacting with smart contracts.
- [Create Polkadot dApp GitHub repo by Paritytech](https://github.com/paritytech/create-polkadot-dapp).

## Constraints

- Integration must maintain backward compatibility with existing QF runtimes and Smart Contracts v0 implementation.
- Emulation for EVM introduces performance trade-offs; optimization is critical.
- EVM compatibility must cover most common Solidity patterns but doesn't need to support every edge case.
- Advanced functions (e.g., ZKP verification) require resource-efficient implementations to avoid slowing execution.
- Performance optimizations must not reduce security guarantees.
- Gas limits must be flexible but prevent block time degradation.
- Formal verification tools must be usable by average developers without specialized knowledge.
- Contract-to-contract calls must maintain proper isolation and security boundaries.

## Risks

- EVM compatibility emulation may underperform compared to native EVM environments.
  - Mitigation: Focus on optimizing the most common operations first and clearly document any performance trade-offs.

- Contract-to-contract call implementation could introduce security vulnerabilities.
  - Mitigation: Implement comprehensive test suite focusing on isolation, input sanitization, and error handling; conduct formal security audit.

- Solidity projects may encounter compatibility or re-certification challenges during porting.
  - Mitigation: Provide detailed migration guides and validation tools to verify functional equivalence after migration.

- EVM compatibility layer could have unexpected behavior with complex contracts.
  - Mitigation: Begin with support for well-established standards (ERC tokens) and gradually expand to more complex patterns; document known limitations.

- RISC-V implementation and integration into QF may require significant development effort.
  - Mitigation: Prioritize core functionality first, establish clear milestones, and consider parallel development tracks.

- Precompiled functions might become bottlenecks under heavy load.
  - Mitigation: Implement resource throttling and benchmark under various load conditions to identify and address potential bottlenecks.

- Performance optimization might introduce new security vulnerabilities.
  - Mitigation: Include security review as part of the optimization cycle and prioritize maintaining security over marginal performance gains.

- Storage rent system could create unexpected economic incentives.
  - Mitigation: Simulate various economic scenarios, start with conservative pricing, and implement mechanisms to adjust parameters through governance.

- Smart contract deployed through PolkaVM might expose vulnerabilities if the deployment process is not correctly validated.
  - Mitigation: Implement comprehensive validation checks during deployment and provide tools to analyze contracts before deployment.

- Performance benchmarks might not reflect real-world usage.
  - Mitigation: Design benchmarks based on actual dApp patterns and include realistic mixed workloads rather than isolated function tests.

- Adapted contracts-ui might not support all required features for QF smart contracts.
  - Mitigation: Prioritize essential features and develop custom components as needed.

## Development Outcomes

- Optimized PolkaVM implementation with documented performance improvements and benchmark results compared to EVM and Wasm.
- Working contract-to-contract call mechanism with comprehensive security measures and documentation.
- Working EVM compatibility layer with verified support for common Solidity patterns and ERC token standards.
- Gas limits research results with optimal values for different contract types under various network conditions.
- Compiler toolchain supporting multiple programming languages with examples and language-specific best practices.
- Advanced precompiles implementation (Merkle proofs, crypto operations) with performance metrics and usage documentation.
- Storage rent system with economic analysis and tuning recommendations.
- Developer tools suite including:
  - Enhanced debugger with source mapping
  - Resource monitoring dashboard
  - Local testing environment
  - Formal verification integration
- Extended documentation covering:
  - Language support and best practices
  - Optimization techniques
  - Security considerations
  - EVM compatibility details
  - Contract-to-contract interaction patterns
  - Storage system economic model
- Smart contract event system implementation with indexing, filtering, and subscription capabilities for dApp integrations.
- Performance analysis toolkit with comparison reports and resource usage statistics.
- Migrated dApp examples from pvm-dapp-demo repository with updated interaction methods.
- Comprehensive dApp development guide with step-by-step tutorials.
- Adapted contracts-ui implementation with QF-specific features and styling.
- Stability and performance test suite with comparison metrics against other platforms.

## Decision Log

- Decision 1: Adopt RISC-V instruction set for PolkaVM implementation.
- Decision 2: Include an EVM compatibility layer to facilitate Solidity-based project migration.
- Decision 3: Prioritize benchmarks and performance analysis as part of acceptance criteria.
- Decision 4: Implementation will build upon the Smart Contracts v0 foundation established in the TestNet case.

## Notes

- This case specifically builds on the foundation of "Smart contract environment for TestNet" and assumes its successful implementation.
- PolkaVM offers significant innovation potential, allowing the execution of diverse programming environments as smart contracts.
- Successful implementation may position QF as a leading platform for high-performance, permissionless smart contract execution.
- Future enhancements may explore further compiler integrations and optimization of advanced precompile functions.

## Learnings
- We use `hash(blob_owner, blob_version)` as an address in the first implementation of smart cantracts addressing (https://github.com/QuantumFusion-network/spec/issues/69) 
- XCQ & PVM: https://github.com/QuantumFusion-network/spec/issues/114

# [IMPROVEMENT] Enhance Documentation and Developer Onboarding Guides for Tornado-SVM

---

## 🚀 Problem Statement

The **Tornado-SVM** project currently suffers from insufficient and unclear documentation and onboarding materials. This creates friction for new contributors, slows down community audits, and hampers the scalability of development efforts. Clear, comprehensive developer guides and contribution instructions are essential to foster a welcoming, productive ecosystem and ensure long-term maintainability of this privacy-centric Solana project.

---

## 🧠 Technical Context

Tornado-SVM is a **Rust-based Solana program** implementing privacy-preserving transactions via zkSNARKs, alongside a JavaScript client interface. The current docs partially cover architecture and usage but lack cohesive developer onboarding paths, clear contribution guidelines, and detailed explanations of cryptographic and Solana-specific patterns used.

The repository includes:
- Rust smart contract code (`program/` folder)
- Client-side JavaScript tooling (`client/`)
- Cryptography and formal verification submodules (`formal_verification/`)
- CI/CD workflows and tests
- Basic README and sparse CONTRIBUTING.md files

Improving developer docs will reduce ramp-up time, improve auditability, and enable the community to confidently contribute and extend the project.

---

## 🔨 Detailed Implementation Steps

1. **Audit Existing Documentation**
   - Review all current docs: README.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, formal_verification docs, Rust doc comments, client docs.
   - Identify gaps: missing onboarding tutorials, unclear setup instructions, outdated contribution processes, lack of code architecture overview.

2. **Create a Developer Onboarding Guide**
   - Write a step-by-step "Getting Started" guide covering:
     - Environment setup (Rust toolchain, Solana CLI, Node.js/npm versions)
     - Building and running the Solana program locally
     - Running the client and example transactions
     - Debugging tips for common issues
   - Include diagrams or flowcharts illustrating the deposit-withdraw zkSNARK flow.

3. **Enhance Contribution Guidelines**
   - Revise CONTRIBUTING.md to detail:
     - Coding standards and Rust style guidelines (e.g., `cargo fmt`, `clippy`)
     - Git branching and commit message conventions
     - Pull request process including required reviews and checks
     - Testing requirements for contributions (unit tests, integration, CI validation)
     - Security best practices for cryptographic code contributions

4. **Document Core Architecture and Security Considerations**
   - Add focused markdown docs explaining:
     - zkSNARK proof generation and verification processes
     - Solana program structure and on-chain state management
     - Formal verification integration and how to run it locally
     - Potential attack surfaces and mitigation strategies

5. **Integrate Documentation in CI/CD**
   - Add a CI job to validate documentation formatting (e.g., markdown linting)
   - Optionally generate and publish documentation site (e.g., using `mdbook` or GitHub Pages)

6. **Update Tests and Examples**
   - Ensure all example code snippets in docs are up-to-date and tested
   - Add new integration test examples illustrating documented workflows

7. **Gather Feedback and Iterate**
   - Share updated docs with internal devs and community contributors for review
   - Incorporate feedback to improve clarity and completeness

---

## 📝 Technical Specifications

- **Documentation format:** Markdown files under `/docs` or root
- **Doc tooling:** Use existing formatting tools (e.g., `prettier` for markdown)
- **Contribution guidelines:** Follow [Rust community standards](https://rust-lang.github.io/api-guidelines/conventions.html)
- **Onboarding environment:** Should cover Solana CLI (version X+), Rust (stable), Node.js (v16+)
- **Diagrams:** Use Mermaid or PlantUML for embedded diagrams in markdown if possible
- **CI Integration:** Add markdown lint step in GitHub Actions workflow
- **Backward Compatibility:** No breaking changes; docs updates only

---

## ✅ Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Comprehensive audit document listing current doc gaps created
- [ ] New `docs/ONBOARDING.md` guide covering environment, build, run, debug workflows
- [ ] Updated `CONTRIBUTING.md` with detailed contribution process and coding standards
- [ ] Architecture and security docs added under `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` and `docs/SECURITY.md`
- [ ] All code examples in docs verified and tested
- [ ] Markdown linting integrated into CI pipeline
- [ ] Documentation reviewed and approved by at least two core maintainers
- [ ] No regressions or build failures introduced

---

## 🧪 Testing Requirements

- Manual verification of onboarding steps on a clean environment (e.g., new VM or container)
- Automated markdown linting and link validation in CI
- Cross-check code snippets compile and run as documented
- Peer review of contribution guidelines for clarity and completeness

---

## 📚 Documentation Updates Required

- Add or revise:
  - `README.md` (overview and links to new docs)
  - `CONTRIBUTING.md` (contribution workflow)
  - `docs/ONBOARDING.md` (developer setup and usage)
  - `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` (system design and flow)
  - `docs/SECURITY.md` (threat model and best practices)
- Update any related wiki pages or GitHub project boards accordingly

---

## ⚠️ Potential Challenges & Risks

- Ensuring onboarding instructions stay up-to-date with rapid codebase changes — consider adding a doc ownership and update schedule.
- Balancing detail with readability to avoid overwhelming new developers.
- Accurately explaining complex cryptographic concepts in approachable language without sacrificing precision.
- Integrating formal verification explanations in a way that is accessible for non-experts.

---

## 🔗 Resources & References

- [Rust API Guidelines](https://rust-lang.github.io/api-guidelines/conventions.html)
- [Solana Developer Docs](https://docs.solana.com/developing)
- [zkSNARKs Primer](https://electriccoin.co/blog/snark-explainer/)
- [GitHub Markdown Lint Action](https://github.com/marketplace/actions/markdownlint)
- Example onboarding guides from similar projects:
  - [Anchor Framework Docs](https://project-serum.github.io/anchor/)
  - [Solana SPL Token Repo](https://github.com/solana-labs/solana-program-library/tree/master/token)

---

Let's turn this cryptographic black box into a developer-friendly rocketship. 🚀 Happy hacking!  
If you have questions or want to pair on docs improvements, ping me anytime!

---

*Part of AI Development Plan Milestone #1*  
*Issue originally opened for openSVM/tornado-svm repository (Rust, zkSNARKs, Solana privacy solution)*

Decision-Making Under Uncertainty: Beyond Probabilities. (arXiv:2303.05848v1 [cs.AI])
https://ift.tt/aibps87

This position paper reflects on the state-of-the-art in decision-making under uncertainty. A classical assumption is that probabilities can sufficiently capture all uncertainty in a system. In this paper, the focus is on the uncertainty that goes beyond this classical interpretation, particularly by employing a clear distinction between aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty. The paper features an overview of Markov decision processes (MDPs) and extensions to account for partial observability and adversarial behavior. These models sufficiently capture aleatoric uncertainty but fail to account for epistemic uncertainty robustly. Consequently, we present a thorough overview of so-called uncertainty models that exhibit uncertainty in a more robust interpretation. We show several solution techniques for both discrete and continuous models, ranging from formal verification, over control-based abstractions, to reinforcement learning. As an integral part of this paper, we list and discuss several key challenges that arise when dealing with rich types of uncertainty in a model-based fashion.

## 🎯 Problem Statement

The current Tornado Cash privacy solution for Solana provides robust unlinkability between deposit and withdrawal addresses using zkSNARKs. However, the **relayer mechanism**—which routes transactions and handles associated fees—has room for significant innovation:

- **Relayer fee management** is currently basic and could be optimized to reduce user costs and improve relayer incentives.
- **Privacy enhancements** at the relayer layer can further obfuscate transaction routing metadata, preventing inference attacks.
- There is an opportunity to **integrate novel features** that enhance relayer efficiency, privacy guarantees, and user experience.

This feature aims to **design, implement, and validate advanced relayer support capabilities** that push the boundaries of privacy and usability in the Tornado Cash ecosystem on Solana.

---

## 🔍 Technical Context

- The project uses **Rust** for the Solana on-chain program and **JavaScript/TypeScript** for client-side tooling (`@solana/web3.js`).
- Current relayer support manages fee payment via simple mechanisms, but lacks:
  - Dynamic fee optimization algorithms
  - Multi-relayer routing or batching
  - Enhanced privacy layers at the relayer level (e.g., cover traffic, transaction mixing)
- The zkSNARK proofs ensure deposit/withdrawal unlinkability but do **not extend to metadata leakage in relayer routing**.
- The ecosystem demands improvements that maintain:
  - Compatibility with Solana’s compute budget
  - Strong cryptographic guarantees
  - Usability for both end-users and relayers

---

## 🛠 Detailed Implementation Steps

### Phase 1: Research & Requirements Gathering  
- [ ] Conduct a **market survey** of existing relayer fee models and privacy-enhancing relayer techniques (e.g., Flashbots MEV relayers, mixnets, threshold relays).
- [ ] Interview community members and relayers to identify pain points and desired features.
- [ ] Document **functional & non-functional requirements** for advanced relayer features, including fee optimization, privacy layers, and UX improvements.

### Phase 2: Architecture & Design  
- [ ] Design a **modular relayer architecture** that supports:
  - Dynamic fee calculation based on network congestion and relayer load
  - Multi-relayer routing with fallback mechanisms
  - Optional privacy enhancements (cover traffic, dummy transactions)
- [ ] Create detailed **sequence diagrams** showing transaction flow with new relayer features.
- [ ] Specify necessary **Solana program interface updates** and off-chain client modifications.
- [ ] Review cryptographic implications and ensure **no weakening of zkSNARK proofs** or privacy guarantees.

### Phase 3: Development Roadmap & MVP  
- [ ] Define MVP scope focusing on **dynamic fee management** and **basic privacy enhancements** (e.g., obfuscated routing metadata).
- [ ] Implement backend changes in the Rust Solana program to support fee flexibility.
- [ ] Extend client SDK (`@solana/web3.js`) to handle new relayer workflows and fee models.
- [ ] Create automated tests for:
  - Fee calculation correctness
  - Privacy feature effectiveness (e.g., metadata obfuscation validation)
- [ ] Integrate the new relayer features into the existing deployment pipeline.

### Phase 4: Feedback & Iteration  
- [ ] Deploy MVP on testnet and invite relayer operators and power users to test.
- [ ] Collect and analyze quantitative (fee savings, latency) and qualitative feedback.
- [ ] Iterate on feature improvements, fixing bugs, and refining UX.

---

## 📋 Technical Specifications

| Feature                     | Details                                                                                           | Notes                                        |
|-----------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------|
| **Dynamic Fee Management**  | Fees are dynamically adjusted based on network load, relayer availability, and transaction size | Use on-chain oracles or off-chain relayer stats |
| **Multi-Relayer Routing**   | Transactions can be routed through multiple relayers with fallback and load balancing           | Design client SDK to select optimal relayer   |
| **Privacy Enhancements**    | Add cover traffic, dummy tx batching, or metadata obfuscation to prevent side-channel leaks     | Balance with Solana compute limits             |
| **Backward Compatibility** | Maintain compatibility with existing deposits/withdrawals and relayer protocols                 | Feature flag new relayer flows                  |
| **Security Guarantees**     | No reduction of zkSNARK proof security; all cryptographic proofs remain valid                    | Formal verification recommended                |

---

## ✅ Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Comprehensive requirements document approved by core devs and community leads
- [ ] Technical design reviewed and merged into the design repository/wiki
- [ ] MVP implemented and passes all unit and integration tests
- [ ] Advanced relayer features deployed on testnet and demonstrated working end-to-end
- [ ] User and relayer feedback collected and documented with action items
- [ ] Updated documentation reflecting new relayer features and usage instructions
- [ ] CI/CD pipeline updated to include new tests and formal verification steps

---

## 🧪 Testing Requirements

- **Unit Tests:**  
  - Fee calculation logic correctness under varied network conditions  
  - Privacy feature toggles and metadata obfuscation modules  

- **Integration Tests:**  
  - Full deposit-withdrawal flow with advanced relayer enabled  
  - Multi-relayer routing fallback and load balancing scenarios  

- **Performance Tests:**  
  - Benchmark gas and compute usage on Solana with new relayer features  
  - Measure latency impact on transactions  

- **Security Audits:**  
  - Formal verification of cryptographic proof compatibility  
  - Penetration testing focusing on metadata leakage in relayer communications  

---

## 📚 Documentation Needs

- Update **Developer Guide** with detailed architecture diagrams and API changes  
- Add **Relayer Operator Manual** explaining fee models, routing, and privacy options  
- Extend **User FAQ** with explanations of how fees are optimized and privacy is enhanced  
- Document **testing and deployment procedures** for new relayer features  

---

## ⚠️ Potential Challenges & Risks

- **Computational Constraints:** Solana’s compute budget per transaction is limited; privacy enhancements must be lightweight and efficient.  
- **Cryptographic Integrity:** Any modification at relayer level must not weaken zkSNARK proof guarantees or introduce side-channel leaks.  
- **User Experience Complexity:** Balancing advanced features with ease of use, especially fee transparency and relayer selection.  
- **Backward Compatibility:** Ensuring existing users and relayers are not broken by changes.  
- **Security Risks:** New relayer routing mechanisms could open attack vectors if not carefully audited.

---

---

## Let's make the relayer ecosystem smarter, stealthier, and way cooler! 🦾🕵️‍♂️  
This is a chance to push privacy tech on Solana beyond the bleeding edge. Let’s build features that future cryptographers will thank us for. 💥

Verified Synthesis of Optimal Safety Controllers for Human-Robot Collaboration. (arXiv:2106.06604v1 [cs.RO])
https://ift.tt/2Tt0K6c

We present a tool-supported approach for the synthesis, verification and validation of the control software responsible for the safety of the human-robot interaction in manufacturing processes that use collaborative robots. In human-robot collaboration, software-based safety controllers are used to improve operational safety, e.g., by triggering shutdown mechanisms or emergency stops to avoid accidents. Complex robotic tasks and increasingly close human-robot interaction pose new challenges to controller developers and certification authorities. Key among these challenges is the need to assure the correctness of safety controllers under explicit (and preferably weak) assumptions. Our controller synthesis, verification and validation approach is informed by the process, risk analysis, and relevant safety regulations for the target application. Controllers are selected from a design space of feasible controllers according to a set of optimality criteria, are formally verified against correctness criteria, and are translated into executable code and validated in a digital twin. The resulting controller can detect the occurrence of hazards, move the process into a safe state, and, in certain circumstances, return the process to an operational state from which it can resume its original task. We show the effectiveness of our software engineering approach through a case study involving the development of a safety controller for a manufacturing work cell equipped with a collaborative robot.



via eess.SY updates on arXiv.org http://arxiv.org/
title: Verified Synthesis of Optimal Safety Controllers for Human-Robot Collaboration. (arXiv:2106.06604v1 [cs.RO])
