# ArXiv AI Research Digest 2026-07-02

> Source: [ArXiv](https://arxiv.org/) (cs.AI, cs.CL, cs.LG) | 50 papers | Generated: 2026-07-02 10:19 UTC

---

# ArXiv AI Research Digest — July 2, 2026

## Today's Highlights

Today's submissions reveal a strong convergence around **test-time adaptation and inference scaling** across multiple domains—from RLHF staleness laws to Monte Carlo reasoning strategies and failure-aware robotics. A second major theme is **structured evaluation**: several papers propose rigorous benchmarks for creativity, sycophancy, safety pragmatics, and video quality, signaling a maturation of LLM assessment beyond simple accuracy. Notably, memory management as a **trainable cognitive skill** (AutoMem, DART-VLN) and the formalization of **agentic supply chains** point toward increasingly systematic approaches to agent architecture. Finally, efficiency innovations—including sub-1-bit KV cache quantization, logarithmic-space quantization, and activation-informed zeroth-order fine-tuning—address practical deployment bottlenecks.

---

## Key Papers

### 🧠 Large Language Models (architecture, training, alignment, evaluation)

**Measuring the Gap Between Human and LLM Research Ideas**  
[arXiv:2607.01233v1](http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01233v1) — Ziyu Chen, Yilun Zhao, Arman Cohan  
*A large-scale evaluation characterizing how far LLM-generated research ideas are from human researchers, moving beyond individual novelty scores to systematic gap analysis.*

**Is One Layer Enough? Training A Single Transformer Layer Can Match Full-Parameter RL Training**  
[arXiv:2607.01232v1](http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01232v1) — Zijian Zhang, Rizhen Hu, Athanasios Glentis et al.  
*Challenges uniform parameter updates in RL post-training by showing that adapting a single transformer layer can match full-parameter performance, with implications for efficient alignment.*

**Right in the Right Way: LM Training with Verifiable Rewards and Human Demonstrations**  
[arXiv:2607.01181v1](http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01181v1) — Mehul Damani, Isha Puri, Idan Shenfeld et al.  
*Extends RL with verifiable rewards to incorporate subjective, non-verifiable quality dimensions via human demonstrations, bridging objective and subjective training signals.*

**Staleness-Learning Rate Scaling Laws for Asynchronous RLHF**  
[arXiv:2607.01083v1](http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01083v1) — Jingwei Song, Haofeng Xu, Jie Xiao et al.  
*Derives scaling laws governing the interaction between rollout staleness and learning rate in asynchronous GRPO, providing principled guidelines for high-throughput RLHF systems.*

**Log\_bQuant: Quantizing Language Models in Logarithmic Space**  
[arXiv:2607.01127v1](http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01127v1) — Jeremias Bohn, Tizian Dippold, Mahdi Koubaa et al.  
*Proposes logarithmic quantization codebooks for LLMs, improving upon uniform quantization for long-tail weight distributions, enabling more efficient deployment on consumer hardware.*

**GSRQ: Gain-Shape Residual Quantization for Sub-1-bit KV Cache**  
[arXiv:2607.01065v1](http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01065v1) — Soosung Kim, Minjae Park, Eui-Young Chung et al.  
*Achieves sub-1-bit per element KV cache compression via gain-shape residual quantization, addressing the memory bottleneck of extended-context LLM inference.*

**Distill to Detect: Exposing Stealth Biases in LLMs through Cartridge Distillation**  
[arXiv:2607.01208v1](http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01208v1) — Shayan Talaei, Abhinav Chinta, Devvrit Khatri et al.  
*Introduces a distillation-based method to detect preferential biases introduced anywhere in the LLM supply chain, particularly dangerous when models reveal preferences only under specific contexts.*

### 🤖 Agents & Reasoning (planning, tool use, multi-agent, chain-of-thought)

**AutoMem: Automated Learning of Memory as a Cognitive Skill**  
[arXiv:2607.01224v1](http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01224v1) — Shengguang Wu, Hao Zhu, Yuhui Zhang et al.  
*Treats memory management for LLM agents as a trainable cognitive skill, elevating file-system operations to first-class actions that decide what to encode, when to retrieve, and how to organize knowledge.*

**Message Passing Enables Efficient Reasoning**  
[arXiv:2607.01077v1](http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01077v1) — Xuecheng Liu, Daman Arora, Gokul Swamy et al.  
*Proposes parallel reasoning via message passing as an alternative to sequential chain-of-thought, enabling fork-join parallelism that reduces inference-time computational bottlenecks.*

**QuasiMoTTo: Quasi-Monte Carlo Test-Time Scaling**  
[arXiv:2607.01179v1](http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01179v1) — Michael Y. Li, Anthony Zhan, Kanishk Gandhi et al.  
*Addresses wasteful redundancy in parallel attempt generation by applying quasi-Monte Carlo methods to diversify LLM outputs at inference time, improving coverage per compute unit.*

**Can Agents Generalize to the Open World? Unveiling the Fragility of Static Training in Tool Use**  
[arXiv:2607.01084v1](http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01084v1) — Song-Lin Lv, Weiming Wu, Rui Zhu et al.  
*Formalizes OpenAgent to study LLM agent generalization under dynamic user queries, tool sets, and interaction dynamics, revealing fundamental fragility of static training.*

**Skills Are Not Islands: Measuring Dependency and Risk in Agent Skill Supply Chains**  
[arXiv:2607.01136v1](http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01136v1) — Changguo Jia, Tianqi Zhao, Runzhi He et al.  
*Identifies and quantifies dependency risks in LLM agent skill ecosystems, showing how implicit versioning and provenance gaps cause duplicated dependencies and inconsistent installations.*

### 🔧 Methods & Frameworks (new techniques, benchmarks, efficiency improvements)

**AGC-Bench: Measuring Artificial General Creativity**  
[arXiv:2607.01152v1](http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01152v1) — Roger Beaty, Vijeta Deshpande, Clin K. Y. Lai et al.  
*Introduces the first unified benchmark for AI creativity across domains (visual, writing, science), testing whether LLMs exhibit domain-specific creativity separable from general intelligence.*

**Adversarial Pragmatics for AI Safety Evaluation**  
[arXiv:2607.01153v1](http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01153v1) — Brett Reynolds  
*A benchmark for evaluating LLMs on ambiguous pragmatic phenomena including instruction conflict, embedded commands, and policy ambiguity, targeting critical failure modes in agentic and safety-critical deployments.*

**Theoria: Rewrite-Acceptability Verification over Informal Reasoning States**  
[arXiv:2607.01223v1](http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01223v1) — Ben Slivinski, Michael Saldivar  
*Bridges formal proof assistants and scalar LLM judges by proposing rewrite-acceptability verification over informal reasoning states, enabling auditable trust judgments without full formalization.*

**CausalMix: Data Mixture as Causal Inference for Language Model Training**  
[arXiv:2607.01104v1](http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01104v1) — Zinan Tang, Yukun Zhang, Shaomian Zheng et al.  
*Frames data mixing as a causal inference problem, learning optimal mixture weights that adapt to distribution shifts without requiring costly proxy model re-evaluation.*

**ZO-Act: Efficient Zeroth-Order Fine-Tuning via One-Shot Activation-Informed Low-Rank Subspaces**  
[arXiv:2607.01125v1](http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01125v1) — Xun Dong, Yibo Xu, Naigang Wang et al.  
*Improves zeroth-order fine-tuning by constructing low-rank subspaces informed by a single forward pass's activations, reducing variance and enabling better performance when backpropagation is unavailable.*

**Conversable Complexity: Agentic LLM Collectives as Interpretable Substrates**  
[arXiv:2607.01047v1](http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01047v1) — Elias Najarro, Ane Espeseth, Eleni Nisioti et al.  
*Shows that collectives of communicating LLM agents can exhibit emergent complex behaviors while remaining interpretable as communication protocols, bridging the complexity-interpretability tradeoff.*

### 📊 Applications (domain-specific, multimodal, code generation)

**FurnitureVLA: Learning Long-Horizon Bimanual Furniture Assembly with Vision-Language-Action Model**  
[arXiv:2607.01212v1](http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01212v1) — Chenyang Ma, Yue Yang, Radu Corcodel et al.  
*First systematic study of real-scale bimanual furniture assembly using VLAs, with a scalable simulation pipeline and real-world transfer, advancing robotic manipulation of complex long-horizon tasks.*

**Cheap Code, Costly Judgment: A Case Study on Governable Agentic Software Engineering**  
[arXiv:2607.01087v1](http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01087v1) — James C. Davis, Paschal C. Amusono, Tanmay Singla et al.  
*Argues that generative AI shifts software engineering's central problem from implementation scarcity to judgment organization, using case studies to explore governable agentic development.*

**Clinician-Level Agreement Without Clinical Caution: LLM Evaluator Limits in Medical AI Benchmarking**  
[arXiv:2607.01103v1](http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01103v1) — William Philipp, Finn Fassbender, Thorsten Langer et al.  
*Introduces MedQADE to evaluate LLM-as-Judge in medical open-response evaluation, finding that LLMs achieve clinician-level agreement but lack clinical calibration and appropriate caution.*

**Agentic generation of verifiable rules for deterministic, self-expanding reaction classification**  
[arXiv:2607.01061v1](http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01061v1) — Daniel Armstrong, Maarten Dobbelaere, Valentas Olikauskas et al.  
*Uses LLM agents to autonomously generate and verify deterministic reaction rules for computer-assisted synthesis planning, addressing the long-tail challenge of manual rule encoding in chemistry.*

---

## Research Trend Signal

A striking pattern across today's submissions is the **formalization of agentic risk and failure modes** as first-class research objects. The emergence of papers on agent skill supply chain dependencies, sycophancy in agent memory, adversarial pragmatics for safety evaluation, and the fragility of static training all point toward a field shifting from "can we build agents?" to "how do we understand, govern, and trust them at scale?" This parallels the maturation of LLM evaluation benchmarks themselves, which now target creativity, clinical caution, and research idea quality rather than simple accuracy. A complementary trend is the **rediscovery of structure** in optimization: logarithmic quantization spaces, causal data mixture formulation, activation-informed subspaces for ZO, and gain-shape residual coding all leverage domain-specific structure to break through the limitations of generic methods. Together, these signals suggest the next phase of AI research will be characterized by structured reasoning about both the artifacts we build and the systems we build them with.

---

## Worth Deep Reading

1. **Theoria: Rewrite-Acceptability Verification over Informal Reasoning States** — This paper directly addresses the fundamental tension between formal verification (too narrow) and LLM-based evaluation (too opaque). Its approach to auditable trust judgments through rewrite-acceptability could become a foundational framework for deploying LLMs in high-stakes domains where "explainability" is not optional.

2. **Conversable Complexity: Agentic LLM Collectives as Interpretable Substrates** — Offers a genuinely novel perspective on the complexity-interpretability trade-off by showing that agent collectives, rather than monolithic models, can be both richly capable and interpretable through their communication protocols. This could reshape how we think about building and auditing complex AI systems.

3. **Can Agents Generalize to the Open World? Unveiling the Fragility of Static Training in Tool Use** — Provides a much-needed formalization of the open-world generalization problem for LLM agents, with concrete failure analyses that will likely become reference points for future work on dynamically adaptive agent architectures.

# LLM Research & Tech Daily Update - 2026-03-04

**3** GitHub updates | **15** arXiv papers | **0** Papers with Code

---

## GitHub Updates (3)

### New Releases

**1. [ollama/ollama](https://github.com/ollama/ollama/releases/tag/v0.17.6)** `v0.17.6`
Relevance: MEDIUM (score: 2.5) | Topics: agent, multimodal

> Ollama v0.17.6 fixes critical issues with GLM-OCR model compatibility and tool calling parsing/rendering for Qwen 3.5 models. This maintenance release resolves prompt rendering problems that prevented GLM-OCR from working properly.

**2. [NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/releases/tag/v1.3.0rc6)** `v1.3.0rc6`
Relevance: LOW (score: 1.7) | Topics: deployment

> TensorRT-LLM v1.3.0rc6 adds support for FLUX.1/FLUX.2 text-to-image pipelines, B300 (sm103) GPU support for VLMs, and quantized Eagle3 model support. The release also includes API improvements with restructured KV cache memory parameters and enhanced visualization tools for performance analysis.

### Trending Repos

**1. [LMCache/LMCache](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache)** | Stars: 7,481 (+135 today)
Relevance: LOW (score: 1.2) | Topics: deployment
Language: Python

> LMCache provides a high-performance KV cache layer designed to supercharge LLM inference speed through optimized caching mechanisms. This project focuses on accelerating large language model deployment by implementing the fastest available KV cache solutions.

---

## arXiv Papers (15)

### 1. [SaFeR-ToolKit: Structured Reasoning via Virtual Tool Calling for Multimodal Safety](http://arxiv.org/abs/2603.02635v1)
**Relevance: HIGH** (score: 5.73) | **Topics**: reasoning, agent, training, multimodal
**Authors**: Zixuan Xu, Tiancheng He, Huahui Yi et al. | **Categories**: cs.LG

> SaFeR-ToolKit introduces a structured protocol for multimodal safety in vision-language models by formalizing safety decisions as checkable tool-calling sequences with Perception→Reasoning→Decision steps. This approach addresses the problem of multimodal jailbreaks and over-refusal by making safety reasoning transparent and verifiable, rather than only supervising final responses.

[PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.02635v1)

### 2. [Graph-GRPO: Stabilizing Multi-Agent Topology Learning via Group Relative Policy Optimization](http://arxiv.org/abs/2603.02701v1)
**Relevance: HIGH** (score: 5.5) | **Topics**: reasoning, coding, agent, training
**Authors**: Yueyang Cang, Xiaoteng Zhang, Erlu Zhao et al. | **Categories**: cs.CL

> Graph-GRPO proposes a Group Relative Policy Optimization approach to stabilize communication topology learning in LLM-based multi-agent systems. This method addresses the severe gradient variance and credit assignment problems that plague existing single-sample policy gradient approaches when optimizing task-specific communication graphs.

[PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.02701v1)

### 3. [Learning When to Act or Refuse: Guarding Agentic Reasoning Models for Safe Multi-Step Tool Use](http://arxiv.org/abs/2603.03205v1)
**Relevance: HIGH** (score: 5.04) | **Topics**: reasoning, agent, training
**Authors**: Aradhye Agarwal, Gurdit Siyan, Yash Pandya et al. | **Categories**: cs.CL

> MOSAIC introduces a post-training framework that aligns agentic language models for safe multi-step tool use by teaching them when to act versus refuse dangerous actions. This addresses a critical safety gap where existing alignment methods fail in sequential decision-making scenarios where single missteps can cause irreversible harm.

[PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.03205v1)

### 4. [AI-for-Science Low-code Platform with Bayesian Adversarial Multi-Agent Framework](http://arxiv.org/abs/2603.03233v1)
**Relevance: HIGH** (score: 4.62) | **Topics**: coding, agent, training
**Authors**: Zihang Zeng, Jiaquan Zhang, Pengze Li et al. | **Categories**: cs.AI

> This work presents a Bayesian adversarial multi-agent framework designed as a low-code platform for AI-for-Science tasks, coordinating three LLM agents (Task Manager, Code Generator, and evaluator) under a Bayesian framework. It addresses reliability challenges and error propagation issues in multi-agent scientific code generation workflows where success metrics are often ill-defined.

[PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.03233v1)

### 5. [RAPO: Expanding Exploration for LLM Agents via Retrieval-Augmented Policy Optimization](http://arxiv.org/abs/2603.03078v1)
**Relevance: HIGH** (score: 4.2) | **Topics**: reasoning, rag, agent
**Authors**: Siwei Zhang, Yun Xiong, Xi Chen et al. | **Categories**: cs.AI

> RAPO introduces Retrieval-Augmented Policy Optimization to expand exploration in LLM agents beyond pure on-policy paradigms by incorporating external knowledge and diverse reasoning perspectives. This addresses the fundamental limitation of existing Agentic RL methods that restrict exploration to self-generated outputs, preventing discovery of new reasoning approaches.

[PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.03078v1)

### 6. [Code2Math: Can Your Code Agent Effectively Evolve Math Problems Through Exploration?](http://arxiv.org/abs/2603.03202v1)
**Relevance: HIGH** (score: 4.1) | **Topics**: reasoning, agent
**Authors**: Dadi Guo, Yuejin Xie, Qingyu Liu et al. | **Categories**: cs.CL

> Code2Math investigates whether code agents can autonomously evolve existing mathematical problems into more complex variations through a multi-agent framework utilizing code execution as a scalable experimentation environment. This addresses the critical bottleneck of scarce high-quality mathematical problems needed for training and evaluating advanced LLMs approaching IMO-level capabilities.

[PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.03202v1)

### 7. [StitchCUDA: An Automated Multi-Agents End-to-End GPU Programing Framework with Rubric-based Agentic Reinforcement Learning](http://arxiv.org/abs/2603.02637v1)
**Relevance: HIGH** (score: 4.1) | **Topics**: coding, agent
**Authors**: Shiyang Li, Zijian Zhang, Winson Chen et al. | **Categories**: cs.MA, cs.CL, cs.PL

> StitchCUDA proposes a multi-agent framework for automated end-to-end GPU program generation, using three specialized agents (Planner, kernel optimizer, and system orchestrator) with rubric-based agentic reinforcement learning. This extends beyond single-kernel optimization to address the complete GPU programming pipeline including host-side settings, which is crucial for practical ML workload deployment.

[PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.02637v1)

### 8. [Saarthi for AGI: Towards Domain-Specific General Intelligence for Formal Verification](http://arxiv.org/abs/2603.03175v1)
**Relevance: MEDIUM** (score: 3.82) | **Topics**: rag, agent
**Authors**: Aman Kumar, Deepak Narayan Gadde, Luu Danh Minh et al. | **Categories**: cs.AI

> Saarthi presents an agentic AI framework using multi-agent collaboration for end-to-end formal verification, achieving around 40% efficacy from specification to coverage closure. While demonstrating promise for domain-specific AGI in formal verification, the work acknowledges significant challenges with LLM hallucinations and reliability that need addressing for robust deployment.

[PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.03175v1)

### 9. [Retrieval-Augmented Robots via Retrieve-Reason-Act](http://arxiv.org/abs/2603.02688v1)
**Relevance: MEDIUM** (score: 3.7) | **Topics**: reasoning, rag, training
**Authors**: Izat Temiraliev, Diji Yang, Yi Zhang | **Categories**: cs.AI, cs.RO

> This work proposes a Retrieve-Reason-Act framework that transforms robots from passive executors into active information retrieval users, addressing critical information gaps in zero-shot settings like furniture assembly. Unlike existing approaches that mainly retrieve past trajectories, this method focuses on retrieving external knowledge to bridge the gap between common sense and complex task requirements.

[PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.02688v1)

### 10. [REGAL: A Registry-Driven Architecture for Deterministic Grounding of Agentic AI in Enterprise Telemetry](http://arxiv.org/abs/2603.03018v1)
**Relevance: MEDIUM** (score: 3.6) | **Topics**: agent, training
**Authors**: Yuvraj Agrawal | **Categories**: cs.AI, cs.SE

> REGAL presents a registry-driven architecture for deterministic grounding of agentic AI systems in enterprise telemetry, addressing challenges of limited model context, locally defined semantics, and evolving metric interfaces. This explicitly architectural approach enables reliable AI automation over high-volume, heterogeneous enterprise data from version control, CI/CD, and observability platforms.

[PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.03018v1)

### 11. [ShipTraj-R1: Reinforcing Ship Trajectory Prediction in Large Language Models via Group Relative Policy Optimization](http://arxiv.org/abs/2603.02939v1)
**Relevance: MEDIUM** (score: 3.54) | **Topics**: reasoning, training
**Authors**: Yang Zhan, Yunhao Li, Zhang Chao et al. | **Categories**: cs.AI

> ShipTraj-R1 introduces a novel LLM-based framework that reformulates ship trajectory prediction as a text-to-text generation problem, enhanced with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) for reinforcement fine-tuning. This represents the first exploration of applying advanced LLM reasoning capabilities to maritime trajectory prediction, using dynamic prompts with conflicting ship information to guide the model.

[PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.02939v1)

### 12. [BrandFusion: A Multi-Agent Framework for Seamless Brand Integration in Text-to-Video Generation](http://arxiv.org/abs/2603.02816v1)
**Relevance: MEDIUM** (score: 3.54) | **Topics**: agent, training
**Authors**: Zihao Zhu, Ruotong Wang, Siwei Lyu et al. | **Categories**: cs.CV, cs.AI

> BrandFusion introduces the first framework for seamless brand integration in text-to-video generation, using a multi-agent system to automatically embed advertiser brands while preserving semantic fidelity and ensuring natural contextual integration. This addresses the largely untapped commercial potential of T2V models by solving the core challenges of prompt fidelity, brand recognizability, and contextual naturalness.

[PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.02816v1)

### 13. [MoD-DPO: Towards Mitigating Cross-modal Hallucinations in Omni LLMs using Modality Decoupled Preference Optimization](http://arxiv.org/abs/2603.03192v1)
**Relevance: MEDIUM** (score: 3.53) | **Topics**: training, multimodal, safety
**Authors**: Ashutosh Chaubey, Jiacheng Pang, Mohammad Soleymani | **Categories**: cs.CV, cs.CL, cs.LG

> MoD-DPO proposes Modality-Decoupled Direct Preference Optimization to mitigate cross-modal hallucinations in omni-modal LLMs by introducing modality-aware regularization terms that enforce invariance to irrelevant modality corruptions. This framework addresses the critical problem of spurious correlations and dominant language priors that make omni LLMs susceptible to hallucinations across audiovisual understanding tasks.

[PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.03192v1)

### 14. [ACE-Brain-0: Spatial Intelligence as a Shared Scaffold for Universal Embodiments](http://arxiv.org/abs/2603.03198v1)
**Relevance: MEDIUM** (score: 3.5) | **Topics**: reasoning, training, multimodal
**Authors**: Ziyang Gong, Zehang Luo, Anke Tang et al. | **Categories**: cs.RO, cs.CL, cs.CV

> ACE-Brain-0 introduces a generalist foundation model that unifies spatial reasoning across heterogeneous embodiments including autonomous driving, robotics, and UAVs, addressing the challenges of long-tail data, gradient interference, and catastrophic forgetting. This work tackles the fundamental problem of balancing universal generalization with domain-specific proficiency in embodied AI systems.

[PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.03198v1)

### 15. [Next Embedding Prediction Makes World Models Stronger](http://arxiv.org/abs/2603.02765v1)
**Relevance: MEDIUM** (score: 3.5) | **Topics**: reasoning, architecture, training
**Authors**: George Bredis, Nikita Balagansky, Daniil Gavrilov et al. | **Categories**: cs.LG, cs.AI

> NE-Dreamer introduces a decoder-free MBRL agent that uses temporal transformers to predict next-step encoder embeddings from latent sequences, enabling learning of coherent predictive representations without reconstruction losses. This approach directly optimizes temporal predictive alignment in representation space, matching or exceeding DreamerV3 performance on DeepMind Control Suite while being more computationally efficient.

[PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.02765v1)

---

### **5. Introduction to Model Checking**

#### **Comprehensive Overview of Model Checking Techniques**

**Model Checking: Definition and Purpose**  
Model checking is a formal verification technique used to ensure the correctness of systems by systematically exploring their state spaces. It verifies that systems adhere to specified properties such as **safety** (avoiding undesirable states), **liveness** (ensuring progress), and **security** (protection against breaches). This technique plays a critical role in **protocol verification** and **complex system design**.

---

### **Model Checking Techniques**

#### 1. **Explicit-State Model Checking**
   - **Definition**: Constructs and explores all states of a system explicitly.
   - **Applications**: Useful for small to moderately complex systems where state spaces are manageable.
   - **Advantages**: Simplicity and effectiveness for finite-state systems.
   - **Challenges**: Suffers from state space explosion for large systems.
   - **Reference**: Holzmann, G.J., "SPIN Model Checker Techniques," *IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering*, 2017. [[[Link](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/8091786)](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/8091786)]

#### 2. **Symbolic Model Checking**
   - **Definition**: Uses symbolic representations like **Binary Decision Diagrams (BDDs)** or **Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT)** to encode state spaces.
   - **Applications**: Effective for handling large state spaces by compactly representing them.
   - **Advantages**: Overcomes explicit-state limitations by reducing memory usage.
   - **Challenges**: Complexity in encoding properties and systems symbolically.
   - **Reference**: Clarke, E.M., et al., "Symbolic Model Checking with SMT Solvers," *IEEE Design & Test of Computers*, 2019. [[[Link](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/8954864)](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/8954864)]

#### 3. **Bounded Model Checking (BMC)**
   - **Definition**: Examines executions of bounded length using propositional logic or SAT solvers.
   - **Applications**: Focuses on detecting bugs within predefined execution bounds.
   - **Advantages**: Scales better than explicit methods and is highly effective in bug detection.
   - **Challenges**: Limited to bounded lengths, making it unsuitable for proving properties universally.
   - **Reference**: Biere, A., "Bounded Model Checking for Hardware Verification," *IEEE Transactions on CAD of Integrated Circuits and Systems*, 2018. [[[Link](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/8306094)](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/8306094)]

#### 4. **Probabilistic Model Checking**
   - **Definition**: Verifies systems with probabilistic behaviors, using Markov chains and similar models.
   - **Applications**: Essential for systems with stochastic processes, like network protocols or fault-tolerant systems.
   - **Advantages**: Models uncertainty and probabilistic guarantees.
   - **Challenges**: Higher computational requirements due to stochastic modeling.
   - **Reference**: Kwiatkowska, M., et al., "Probabilistic Model Checking for Complex Systems," *IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering*, 2019. [[[Link](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/8927093)](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/8927093)]

#### 5. **Temporal Logic-Based Model Checking**
   - **Definition**: Expresses system properties using **Linear Temporal Logic (LTL)** or **Computation Tree Logic (CTL)** for verification.
   - **Applications**: Verifies both linear and branching behaviors of systems.
   - **Advantages**: Expressive frameworks for specifying complex temporal properties.
   - **Challenges**: Complexity in writing temporal logic formulas for non-trivial properties.
   - **Reference**: Vardi, M.Y., et al., "Applications of Temporal Logic in Verification," *IEEE Computer Society Press*, 2020. [[[Link](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/9298546)](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/9298546)]

---

### **6. Scope and Contributions**

- **Focus**: Model checking as a formal method for verifying communication protocols.  
- **Key aspects covered**:  
  - Analyzing the state-of-the-art in model checking for protocol verification.  
  - Practical applications in ensuring the security and reliability of protocols.  
  - Addressing challenges and exploring emerging trends.  
- **Objective**: To bridge the gap between theoretical foundations and real-world implementations of model checking.

**References**:  
[[Formal Verification of Protocol Specifications](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/479337)](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/479337)  
[[Profiling and Validation Using Model Checking](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/5671736)](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/5671736)

body:
### RFP ID

RFP-008 — Lending & Borrowing Protocol

### Your Project Name

Tokos

### Team or Organization Name

CleevioX

### Primary Contact

damsky@cleevio.com

### Team Members

This work is submitted by CleevioX as a company. The delivery shape is a **lean core team of 2-3 engineers**, with additional internal support for review, frontend integration, QA, and delivery management when needed.

Keeping the core team small is deliberate: protocol work of this kind benefits from tight ownership over the accounting and state model. Support can be added around the edges without turning the core protocol into a coordination-heavy project.

**Team members**

| Name | Role | Status | Links |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Daniel Rolník | Technical lead — protocol design, accounting/share math, Rust/SPEL, liquidation & flash-loan logic | Full-time (CleevioX) | https://github.com/rolnimar, https://www.linkedin.com/in/rolnik-daniel/ |
| Sebastian Jakabcin | Core engineer — Rust/SPEL program, instruction handlers, integration | Full-time (CleevioX) | https://www.linkedin.com/in/sebastian-jakabcin-6a28b1220/ |
| Tomáš Krasoň | Core engineer — client core, CLI/GUI, reference tooling | Full-time (CleevioX) | https://www.linkedin.com/in/tkrason/ |

> Additional CleevioX support (review, frontend integration, QA, delivery management) is available around the core team as needed.

### Project Summary

This proposal is to build RFP-008 as a **Morpho Blue-style isolated-market lending protocol for LEZ**, delivered as production-ready software.

The protocol is a **singleton Rust/SPEL lending program**. Markets are isolated and defined by five immutable parameters: loan token, collateral token, oracle, IRM, and LLTV. Users can create markets, supply, withdraw, deposit collateral, borrow, repay, and liquidate unhealthy positions. The program tracks internal supply and borrow shares, accrues interest lazily, uses AdaptiveCurveIRM, keeps market parameters immutable, and contains bad debt inside the affected market.

**The goal is not to redesign lending.** The RFP already points at Morpho Blue, and that is the right base design for LEZ: a small immutable core, isolated markets, a minimal governance surface, and a periphery that can grow later. Morpho Blue is used as the reference for behavior and accounting, but the implementation is **independent Rust/SPEL code for LEZ — Solidity source will not be copied**.

SPEL and the surrounding LEZ APIs are still moving. Freezing this work to a single framework commit today is not realistic, so the project follows SPEL from the start and absorbs framework changes during development. The protocol is written as a SPEL-native program, with pure Rust used where it is useful for deterministic math, accounting helpers, and test vectors. SPEL is the programming model we build against, not a wrapper added at the end.

Scope stays tight and close to the Morpho-style core — it does not expand into RFP-012 vaults, hosted indexing, governance, oracle-provider work, or production operations.

**Why this matters.** Lending is the capital-efficiency engine of a DeFi ecosystem: it unlocks idle assets, lets holders earn yield, and gives borrowers liquidity without selling. The Morpho Blue model fits a nascent ecosystem like LEZ specifically because permissionless market creation removes governance bottlenecks for listing assets, isolated markets stop bad debt cascading between markets, and a minimal immutable core is far easier to audit, formally verify, and reason about — which matters most when the protocol is the first lending primitive on a new chain. Beyond TVL, lending creates the borrowing market for stablecoins and the collateral layer that synthetic assets and structured products are later built on.

### Technical Approach

### Morpho Blue model on LEZ

The proposal stays inside the Morpho Blue boundary: an immutable singleton core for isolated markets, plus the minimum client and reference tooling needed to use it on LEZ. It does not expand into vaults, governance products, looping, native stablecoin issuance, or hosted protocol operations.

**Data-model translation:**

| Morpho Blue | LEZ |
| --- | --- |
| singleton `Morpho.sol` | singleton Rust/SPEL lending program |
| `MarketParams` | LEZ market params struct/account data |
| `Id = hash(MarketParams)` | deterministic market id |
| `Market` totals | market state keyed by market id |
| `Position` mapping | position state keyed by market id and owner |
| ERC20 transfers | LEZ token program calls through chained calls |
| callbacks / flash loans | LEZ tail-call / chained-call continuation model |
| events | LEZ structured events for reference tools |

**Behavior boundary:**

| Morpho Blue behavior | LEZ proposal boundary |
| --- | --- |
| One immutable core contract | One immutable SPEL lending program |
| Markets defined by loan token, collateral token, oracle, IRM, LLTV | Same five-parameter market model adapted to LEZ account IDs |
| Permissionless market creation; LLTV/IRM choices enabled by admin | Same: anyone creates a market from enabled LLTV/IRM values |
| Market parameters immutable after creation | Same: no market-mutation instruction |
| Oracle-agnostic core, trusts the market's selected oracle | Same: oracle quality/freshness policy lives in the oracle program, not the core |
| Supply/borrow tracked with internal shares | Same: no receipt token at the core layer |
| Collateral tracked separately from supplied loan-token shares | Same |
| Permissionless liquidation when LTV exceeds LLTV | Same |
| No close factor on standard liquidation | Same |
| Liquidator specifies debt-to-repay or collateral-to-seize | Same |
| LIF derived from LLTV | Same Morpho-style formula and constants from the RFP |
| Bad debt isolated to the affected market | Same |
| `setAuthorization` / signature authorization for delegated management | Same concept via LEZ-native authorization and signature path |
| Zero-fee, atomically repaid flash loans | Same, via LEZ tail-call / chained-call continuation |
| Vaults are a separate layer | Out of scope here; deferred to RFP-012 |

Market state follows the same accounting shape: total supplied assets, total supply shares, total borrowed assets, total borrow shares, last-update timestamp, and fee. A position stores supply shares, borrow shares, and collateral for one market. The important part is conversions and rounding: supply and borrow shares use **virtual shares/assets or an equivalent protection** against donation and first-depositor attacks, and collateral is tracked separately from yield-bearing supply shares.

### Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  User[User / liquidator / admin] --> Client[Client core]
  Client --> CLI[CLI]
  Client --> GUI[Basecamp module]
  Client --> Bot[Liquidator / monitor]

  Client --> Tx[LEZ transaction]
  Tx --> Lending[SPEL lending singleton]

  Lending --> Config[Protocol config]
  Lending --> Market[Market state]
  Lending --> Position[Position state]
  Lending --> Delegate[Delegation state]

  Lending -- chained calls --> Token[LEZ token program]
  Lending -- price read --> Oracle[Oracle program]
  Lending -- rate read --> IRM[AdaptiveCurveIRM program]

  Multisig[lez-multisig] -- approved chained call --> Lending
```

**Account model:**

| Account / state | Purpose | Expected contents |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ProtocolConfig` | Global protocol config | admin authority, enabled LLTV set, enabled IRM set, protocol fee, fee recipient |
| `MarketParams` | Immutable market identity | loan token, collateral token, oracle program, IRM program, LLTV |
| `MarketState` | Mutable market totals | total supply assets/shares, total borrow assets/shares, last accrual timestamp, fee data |
| `Position` | User position in one market | owner, market id, supply shares, borrow shares, collateral amount |
| `DelegateApproval` | Optional delegated management | owner, delegate, market or global scope, nonce/enable flag |
| `FlashLoanCapability` | Transaction-scoped repayment guard | principal, token, repayment continuation/capability; no persistent market-level policy |
| `OracleMetadata` | Only if required by canonical oracle API | return shape and scaling metadata; no freshness policy in the lending core |

**Deterministic IDs** follow Morpho's `id = hash(MarketParams)` pattern, adapted to LEZ account derivation:

```
market_id           = hash(loan_token, collateral_token, oracle, irm, lltv)
market_state_id     = derive_account("market", market_id)
position_account_id = derive_account("position", market_id, owner)
delegate_account_id = derive_account("delegate", owner, delegate)
```

Exact seed format follows the current SPEL/LEZ convention at implementation time. The design requirement is deterministic addressing, stable off-chain derivation, and no mutable market parameters after creation.

### RFP requirement mapping

| RFP requirement | Implementation expectation |
| --- | --- |
| singleton lending protocol | one SPEL lending program owns all markets |
| immutable core | no upgrade, pause, migration, or market-mutation instruction |
| permissionless markets | `create_market(params)` derives `market_id` and initializes if LLTV/IRM are enabled |
| supply / withdraw | internal supply shares; token custody via chained calls |
| borrow / repay | internal borrow shares; LLTV check against oracle price |
| AdaptiveCurveIRM | separate immutable LEZ IRM program with deterministic fixed-point math |
| lazy interest | every market-mutating instruction calls `accrue_interest(market)` first |
| liquidation | permissionless instruction; Morpho-style LIF derived from LLTV; no close factor |
| bounded admin | admin only enables LLTVs/IRMs and sets fee recipient/fraction |
| protocol fee | capped at 25% of accrued interest in immutable code |
| flash loans | zero-fee LEZ tail-call/chained-call repayment; exact principal repayment |
| delegated management | owner-authorized delegate plus signature-based authorization path |
| reference tooling | CLI, Basecamp module, liquidator, risk monitor, docs, test vectors |

### Instruction and account map

| Instruction | Main accounts | Chained calls | Main checks |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `initialize_config` | config, admin | none | config not initialized, admin signer |
| `enable_lltv` / `disable_lltv` | config, admin | none | admin authorized, LLTV valid; removal affects only future market creation |
| `enable_irm` | config, admin, IRM program id | none | admin authorized, IRM interface accepted |
| `set_fee` | config, admin, fee recipient | none | admin authorized, fee ≤ 25% cap |
| `create_market` | config, market state | none | LLTV enabled, IRM enabled, market does not exist |
| `supply` | market, position, user loan holding, market loan custody | transfer loan token user → custody | accrue interest; shares rounded against supplier |
| `withdraw` | market, position, receiver loan holding, market loan custody | transfer loan token custody → receiver | accrue interest; enough shares; enough liquidity |
| `deposit_collateral` | market, position, user collateral holding, market collateral custody | transfer collateral user → custody | collateral token matches market |
| `withdraw_collateral` | market, position, receiver collateral holding, market collateral custody, oracle | transfer collateral custody → receiver | accrue interest; post-withdraw LTV ≤ LLTV |
| `borrow` | market, position, receiver loan holding, market loan custody, oracle | transfer loan token custody → receiver | accrue interest; liquidity; post-borrow LTV ≤ LLTV |
| `repay` | market, position, payer loan holding, market loan custody | transfer loan token payer → custody | accrue interest; debt share conversion |
| `liquidate` | market, borrower position, liquidator holdings, custody, oracle | transfer repay token in, transfer seized collateral out | position unhealthy; exactly one of repay/seize; LIF math; bad-debt handling |
| `set_authorization` | owner, delegate approval | none | owner signer; scope encoded |
| `set_authorization_with_sig` | owner, delegate approval, submitter | none | valid owner signature; replay protection |
| `revoke_authorization` | owner, delegate approval | none | owner signer |
| `flash_loan` | token liquidity/custody, borrower receiver, repayment continuation | transfer out, borrower continuation, repayment continuation | zero fee; exact principal repaid before transaction end |

Final names may follow SPEL conventions, but this is the expected behavior surface. **Every token movement is owned by the lending instruction and emitted as a LEZ chained call** — the user never composes token transfers that bypass protocol accounting.

### Oracle, IRM, and token movement (integrations)

The lending core uses the oracle selected by each market and does not judge oracle quality inside the lending program — matching the RFP and the Morpho trust model, where lenders choose which markets and oracles they trust. Development and tests use a **mock oracle**; production integrates with the **canonical oracle interface** once available on LEZ. Oracle freshness, heartbeat, confidence, and manipulation policy stay inside the oracle program a market selects.

**AdaptiveCurveIRM** is the launch IRM, implemented as a separate immutable LEZ program with deterministic fixed-point math and test vectors, so economic behavior can be reviewed independently of framework mechanics. The IRM exposes pure read functions returning supply APY and borrow APR for a market id; no state mutation is required to query rates.

Token movement (supply, borrow, repay, liquidation, fee accounting, flash loans) runs through the **LEZ token program via chained calls** rather than Solana CPI. The chained-call model is treated as the LEZ-native equivalent of CPI:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User transaction
  participant L as Lending program
  participant O as Oracle / IRM
  participant T as LEZ token program
  participant E as LEZ executor

  U->>L: call lending instruction with required accounts
  L->>O: read price / rate where needed
  L->>L: accrue interest and compute state transition
  L->>T: emit chained token call(s)
  T->>T: validate token authority and balances
  E->>E: validate full chained execution
  E-->>U: commit all state or revert all state
```

### Client, CLI, GUI

A reusable **Rust client core** is built first: account decoding, transaction construction, market/position queries, LTV calculation, and projected-LTV previews. The CLI and GUI both consume that same client core. The CLI covers all core flows (create/inspect market, inspect position, supply, withdraw, deposit/withdraw collateral, borrow, repay, liquidate).

The GUI is a **functional Logos/Basecamp module** (QML + C++), with the core module and GUI module buildable independently, as the RFP requires. The QML/C++ layer stays thin and follows Basecamp conventions; lending logic lives in the shared client and program. Both CLI and GUI surface oracle program IDs, current supply APY, borrow APR, utilisation, current LTV, and **projected LTV** before borrow and collateral-withdrawal flows. Local build instructions, GUI assets, and Figma (or equivalent) designs are part of the handoff.

### Liquidator, monitor, private flow

The project ships **reference tooling** (runnable, not a commitment to operate after launch):

- a **liquidator daemon** that watches positions and submits liquidations;
- a **risk monitor** that reports utilisation, LTV bands, oracle status, and bad-debt/solvency data via API or dashboard.

The lending state itself is public — required for composability, oracle use, and permissionless liquidation. The **private-account path lives in the SDK/client layer**: deshield token amount plus native gas as one atomic user action, interact through a fresh single-use public account, then reshield outputs. The SDK enforces fee/balance prechecks, validates that the reshield target is private, prevents ephemeral-account reuse, and makes the reshield step non-skippable. A **privacy document** explains what is public, what is private, and which guarantees depend on the client versus the platform.

### Security and admin model

The lending core has a small admin surface: enabling/disabling LLTV values for future markets, enabling IRM implementations, and setting protocol fee parameters. **The admin cannot control user funds, mutate live market parameters, pause lending, upgrade the program, or migrate markets.** This scope does not rebuild a Squads-like multisig inside the protocol; the program exposes explicit admin instructions compatible with the Logos-designated admin authority, including `lez-multisig` if Logos selects it.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant M as Multisig member
  participant MS as lez-multisig
  participant L as Lending program

  M->>MS: propose target = lending.enable_lltv / enable_irm / set_fee
  M->>MS: approve proposal
  MS->>MS: threshold reached
  MS->>L: execute approved chained call
  L->>L: verify configured admin authority
  L->>L: update ProtocolConfig only
```

The lending program does not know `lez-multisig`'s internal voting rules; it only verifies that the caller holds the configured admin authority. This keeps the protocol independent from the final mainnet governance choice while remaining compatible with the Logos multisig path.

### Anticipated challenges and risk management

The largest delivery risk is **framework and platform movement** around SPEL, LEZ APIs, token authority, oracle interfaces, private-account support, and Basecamp. The approach:

- build against SPEL from the beginning and track SPEL/LEZ API changes continuously, rather than pinning to a stale commit;
- keep deterministic math and accounting helpers easy to test and review;
- integrate with **testnet early** and keep a working testnet path throughout (Logos already has testnet running);
- use mock oracle/token adapters until canonical interfaces are ready;
- keep sequencer E2E tests for critical flows;
- keep GUI logic thin and shared with the CLI through the Rust client core;
- maintain a requirement-coverage matrix in the repo.

Critical review areas — given they are the parts most likely to cause loss — are share accounting, rounding, interest accrual, liquidation math, oracle assumptions, token custody, flash-loan repayment, and bad-debt handling. Each gets explicit tests and review notes.

**Compute-budget risk:** liquidation is the most compute-intensive operation. We benchmark liquidation compute and transaction size on LEZ testnet once integrated, report figures in the README, and — if liquidation does not fit the per-transaction budget — implement a remediation (e.g. two-phase liquidation via tail-call continuation) within the funded scope.

If a required platform piece is missing completely, or if expected scope changes materially, the response is to discuss tradeoffs with Logos rather than cut safety-critical protocol work. If the moving LEZ/SPEL surface consumes more time than expected, the first trade-off is polish in GUI/reference tooling — never protocol accounting, liquidation safety, tests, or private-account correctness.

### LEZ/SPEL ramp-up

Part of the work is validating the current LEZ application model in practice. The team has relevant Solana/Rust experience, but LEZ is not Solana: SPEL code generation, LEZ account validation, chained calls, RISC0 guest execution, Basecamp integration, and private-account UX all need hands-on work. This ramp-up happens **through implementation, not as a separate research phase** — start with a small SPEL program and client flow to confirm build/IDL/account derivation/sequencer execution, build token-transfer and chained-call examples before wiring full lending flows, validate private-account deshield/interact/reshield as soon as the wallet APIs are available, stay in close feedback with Logos engineers when APIs move, and turn findings into repository developer notes and runbooks. The protocol is built while continuously learning against the live LEZ/SPEL stack, not ported at the end from a Solana-shaped design.

### Scope boundaries

**In scope:** the lending protocol and the surrounding software needed to deploy and use it on testnet and prepare it for production — client core, CLI, functional GUI, liquidator, risk monitor, tests, benchmarks, docs, audit/formal-verification support, and deployment handoff material. Market creation, lending, borrowing, repayment, withdrawal, liquidation, interest accrual, AdaptiveCurveIRM, delegated management, and flash loans are all included.

**Out of scope** (per the RFP):

- platform pieces owned by other Logos workstreams (oracle-provider implementation, LEZ runtime changes, wallet changes, Basecamp platform changes);
- post-launch operations (hosting liquidators/monitors, 24/7 support, incident response, market-risk operations);
- third-party security-vendor execution and vendor fees — the engineering scope includes audit preparation, formal-verification support for the RFP invariants, and remediation planning; commercial audit budget and vendor engagement are handled privately with Logos;
- product layers outside RFP-008 — especially RFP-012 curated vaults, governance, native stablecoin issuance, cross-chain liquidity, looping, and off-chain indexing.


### Milestones, Payout and Timeline

The work is delivered in **six milestones**. Each milestone is a reviewable, independently verifiable outcome with a defined "done" condition, so Logos can track and release per milestone.

**Payout.** Total requested is **$182,650**, split across the six milestones below. Each milestone is released on completion of its deliverables.

**Timeline.** Indicative durations total roughly **22 weeks**, against the RFP's 16-week estimate. The schedule can compress with more engineers in parallel; final duration and staffing are open for discussion. A working testnet path is exercised throughout, so the order below is a planning order, not strict sequential delivery. 


> **Disclaimer.** The milestones, scopes, durations, and payouts below are a **rough estimate**. Given the moving SPEL/LEZ surface and the breadth of the build, the exact milestone boundaries and scope will be defined together with Logos before work starts; the figures are a basis for that discussion, not a fixed commitment.

### Milestone 1 — Foundation, state & accounting core
**Deliverables:**
- SPEL program skeleton, IDL surface, generated client bindings, deterministic account-derivation helpers; small client flow and sequencer execution confirmed on **LEZ testnet** (this folds the ramp-up into delivery, not a separate research phase).
- Core state model: `ProtocolConfig`, `MarketParams`, `MarketState`, `Position`, `DelegateApproval`; deterministic market ids.
- Accounting primitives: fixed-point math, supply/borrow share conversions with **virtual shares/assets (or equivalent) donation- and first-depositor-attack resistance**, lazy interest accrual, fee accrual.
- Invariant and unit tests for share math, rounding, and accrual; chained-call examples for token movement.

**Done when:** state model and accounting helpers are implemented with passing invariant tests, and the skeleton program builds, derives accounts, and executes on testnet.
**Duration:** ~4.5 weeks. **Payout:** $37,700

### Milestone 2 — Core market flows, IRM & oracle
**Deliverables:**
- SPEL instruction handlers and account validation for `create_market`, `supply`, `withdraw`, `deposit_collateral`, `withdraw_collateral`, `borrow`, `repay`, with all token movement owned by the lending program and emitted as **LEZ chained calls** to the token program (custody accounts).
- **AdaptiveCurveIRM** as a separate immutable LEZ program: deterministic fixed-point rate math, pure read interface (supply APY / borrow APR), and test vectors reviewable independently of framework mechanics.
- Oracle integration through the canonical oracle interface, developed against a **mock oracle** first, with price shape/scaling validation; LLTV health checks gating borrow and collateral withdrawal.
- Unit tests for flow math plus sequencer-level tests for account ownership and chained token movement.

**Done when:** the full non-liquidation market lifecycle works end-to-end on testnet with IRM-driven rates and oracle-fed health checks, covered by unit and sequencer tests.
**Duration:** ~4.5 weeks. **Payout:** $36,400

### Milestone 3 — Liquidation, delegation & flash loans
**Deliverables:**
- Permissionless `liquidate` with Morpho-style **LIF derived from LLTV** (β = 0.3, max M = 1.15), **no close factor**, liquidator specifies exactly one of debt-to-repay or collateral-to-seize, with **bad-debt socialisation contained to the affected market**.
- Delegated position management: `set_authorization`, `revoke_authorization`, and a **signature-based `set_authorization_with_sig`** path with replay protection.
- **Zero-fee flash loans** via the LEZ tail-call / chained-call continuation model with an unforgeable repayment capability and exact principal repayment, reverting atomically if unrepaid.
- Tests covering healthy-position liquidation rejection, unhealthy liquidation, LIF bounds, bad-debt handling, delegation scope, and flash-loan repayment/abort.

**Done when:** liquidation, delegation, and flash loans pass their safety and accounting tests on testnet.
**Duration:** ~2.5 weeks. **Payout:** $20,800

### Milestone 4 — Client core, CLI & Basecamp GUI
**Deliverables:**
- Reusable **Rust client core**: account derivation, transaction builders, market/position decoding, LTV and **projected-LTV previews** — the single source of truth reused by CLI, GUI, and reference tooling.
- **CLI** covering all core flows (create/inspect market, inspect position, supply, withdraw, deposit/withdraw collateral, borrow, repay, liquidate).
- Functional **QML/C++ Basecamp GUI module**, buildable independently from the core module, surfacing oracle program IDs, supply APY, borrow APR, utilisation, current and projected LTV; GUI assets and Figma (or equivalent) designs included.
- **Private-account UX**: atomic deshield (token + native gas) as one action, fresh single-use ephemeral account, non-skippable reshield, fee/balance prechecks, and reshield-target-is-private validation, with per-operation pre-confirmation summaries of what is public vs private.

**Done when:** CLI and GUI both drive the full protocol through the shared client core, including the enforced private-account path, with local build instructions for the Logos app.
**Duration:** ~4 weeks. **Payout:** $31,200

### Milestone 5 — Reference tooling, tests, benchmarks & docs
**Deliverables:**
- Reference **liquidator daemon** (watches positions, submits liquidations) and **risk monitor** (utilisation, LTV bands, oracle status, bad-debt/solvency) exposed via API/dashboard, both headless on the shared client core and forkable by third parties.
- Full test suite: unit + **E2E tests against the LEZ sequencer in CI**, green default branch, and a **requirement-coverage matrix** (≥1 test per hard requirement).
- **Transaction-size and liquidation compute benchmarks** on LEZ testnet, with reported max supported market count and a remediation (e.g. two-phase liquidation) if liquidation does not fit the per-transaction budget.
- Documentation: README (deployment, addresses, CLI/GUI usage), **SDK doc packet**, **CLI doc packet**, and the **privacy/anonymisation properties document**.

**Done when:** reference tooling runs against testnet, CI is green with full requirement coverage, benchmarks are reported, and docs are complete.
**Duration:** ~4 weeks. **Payout:** $30,550

### Milestone 6 — Security, audit & formal-verification support, production handoff
**Deliverables:**
- **Support for formal verification** of the required core invariants (no liquidation below LLTV; supply-share value monotonic non-decreasing absent socialised bad debt; IRM borrow rate monotonic non-decreasing in utilisation; protocol solvency), working alongside a specialist firm — we prepare the spec, properties, and harness rather than owning the verification engagement end-to-end.
- **Audit support**: security review notes, deterministic build notes, testnet deployment scripts, engagement coordination with at least one tier-1 firm, and remediation planning. A second independent audit of the lending program is strongly preferred given immutability.
- **Candidate firms:** Trail of Bits, OpenZeppelin, Spearbit, Cantina, ChainSecurity, Certora, Halborn.
- Deployment handoff material for Logos' separate production-deployment process.

**Done when:** the formal-verification and audit engagements are supported through to remediation planning, and the production-readiness handoff package is delivered.
**Duration:** ~3 weeks. **Payout:** $26,000

> **Note on audit vendor fees.** This milestone covers our *support* for the audit and formal-verification work — preparation, coordination, and remediation planning. The **external audit firm's fees are separate** and are scoped and contracted directly with Logos; they are not part of the $182,650 total. Audit cost depends on the firm and final scope, so we do not estimate it here.

**Milestone summary**

| # | Milestone | Duration | Payout |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Foundation, state & accounting core | ~4.5 weeks | $37,700 |
| 2 | Core market flows, IRM & oracle | ~4.5 weeks | $36,400 |
| 3 | Liquidation, delegation & flash loans | ~2.5 weeks | $20,800 |
| 4 | Client core, CLI & Basecamp GUI | ~4 weeks | $31,200 |
| 5 | Reference tooling, tests, benchmarks & docs | ~4 weeks | $30,550 |
| 6 | Security, audit & formal-verification support, handoff | ~3 weeks | $26,000 |
| | **Total** | **~22 weeks** | **$182,650** |

> A more granular breakdown of milestone deliverables is available on request.


### Total Requested Budget (USD)

$182,650

### Relevant Experience

The closest reference project is **`onre-sol`**, a larger Solana/Anchor codebase the team has been building and hardening. It is not a lending protocol, but it exercises the same engineering: token custody and routing, PDA-heavy state, SPL Token / Token-2022 integration, vault flows, configurable authorities, pricing logic, Rust integration tests with LiteSVM, CLI/scripts, and audit-style cleanup.

That experience transfers to LEZ because the mental model is the same: explicit accounts, program-owned state, deterministic addresses, token-program composition, and local/testnet integration tests. The parts that do **not** transfer 1:1 — SPEL, chained calls, RISC0 guest execution, Basecamp integration, and private-account UX — are accounted for in the plan rather than treated as "Solana with different names."

**Links:**
- onre-sol (Solana/Anchor codebase): https://github.com/onre-finance/onre-sol
- OnRe live product: https://app.onre.finance

### Post-Delivery Plan

CleevioX provides a stabilization period after delivery — handoff support, bug triage, minor fixes, and coordination with Logos engineering.

Beyond that, CleevioX is committed to building and growing the protocol, not just shipping it and stepping away. As its original authors, we intend to keep a dedicated team on it — maintaining and upgrading the core, delivering follow-on scope such as the RFP-012 vault layer and additional IRMs, and driving real adoption through integrations, TVL, and ecosystem traction. We will commit the people and effort to make it a leading lending protocol on LEZ and a credible one across Web3.

### Permissions and Consent

- [x] I confirm Logos may contact me using the primary contact information provided above for follow-ups and next steps.
- [x] I consent to Logos using information from this proposal publicly such as blogs case studies social posts or analytical reporting. Redactions can be requested at any time.

### Program Requirements

- [x] We understand this project must be open-sourced under the MIT and Apache 2.0 Licenses unless explicitly approved otherwise.
- [x] We are prepared to deliver milestone-based outcomes.

### 著者/所属機関
Byron Cook (Amazon Web Services, University College London)

### 出典
FLoC 2018 (CAV 2018)

- FLoC Plenary Lecture (CAV 2018 Invited Paper)
  - AWSでの形式手法の活用について
  - Open Accessのため↓で閲覧可能
    - [Formal Reasoning About the Security of Amazon Web Services \| SpringerLink](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-319-96145-3_3)
  - 講演の映像も↓から視聴可能
    - [Formal Reasoning about the Security of Amazon Web Services \| University of Oxford Podcasts - Audio and Video Lectures](https://podcasts.ox.ac.uk/formal-reasoning-about-security-amazon-web-services)

## 内容
- AWSでは分散アルゴリズムの設計に形式手法(TLA+)を使用 (2014)
- 本論文では特にAWSでのセキュリティに形式手法を用いた事例を紹介

### Security of the Cloud: Where Formal Reasoning Fits In
- AWS内部の開発，特にセキュリティレビューで定理証明やモデル検査(symbolic model checking)の利用が増えている
- 2017年だけでも下記の事例にて定理証明やモデル検査を適用
  - [s2n](https://github.com/awslabs/s2n) (TLS/SSL実装)の検証
    - ちなみにこの内容の論文が同会議にて発表されている
    - [Continuous Formal Verification of Amazon s2n \| SpringerLink](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-319-96142-2_26)
  - ハイパーバイザ，ブートローダ，BIOS，ファームウェアの検証
    - こっちも同会議で発表あり
    - [Model Checking Boot Code from AWS Data Centers \| SpringerLink](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-319-96142-2_28)
  - ガーベッジコレクタ
  - ネットワーク設計
- OSSを活用しつつ使う上で生じた変更をフィードバックしており，例えば下記を利用+貢献
  - [CBMC](https://www.cprover.org/cbmc/): C/C++向けのbounded model checker
  - [SAW](https://saw.galois.com): CやJabaでの特定性質の検証
  - [SMACK](http://smackers.github.io/): Cプログラムに対するアサーション検証
- s2nなど一部プロジェクトでは形式検証ツールをCI/CDに組み込み，継続的検証を実施
- SMT-basedのツールで設定ミス防止を図っている
- 形式手法の利用はコードを書く前から始まっている＝プロトコルやアルゴリズムの設計段階から利用

### Securing Customers _in_ the Cloud
- AWS利用者側に対しても形式手法の適用が始まっている
  - 例えば，S3の公開設定ミスを警告する機能をSMTソルバを用いて実現
    - おそらく↓の話
    - [How AWS uses automated reasoning to help you achieve security at scale \| AWS Security Blog](https://aws.amazon.com/jp/blogs/security/protect-sensitive-data-in-the-cloud-with-automated-reasoning-zelkova/)
  - AWS Macieでも同様のツールを利用
  - 複雑なネットワーク設定時の到達性(おそらくルーティングや通信可否)をdatalogを用いて検証

### その他
- 他社事例(文献)として以下に言及 (抜粋)
  - IBM, Google @ Dagstuhl Seminar 2013
  - Microsoft @ SOSP 2015 分散システムの検証
  - Facebook @ LICS 2018 codebaseの継続的検証

### Challenges
- Reasonign About Risk and Feasibility: セキュリティエンジニアは大半の時間を"informal"なリスク分析に使ってる→Formalにしていきたい
- Fixes Not Findings: 見つけるだけじゃなく直し方まで合わせて自動化していきたい (synthesis技術など)
- Auditable Proof Artifacts for Compliance: mechanical proofでチェックできる部分もある
- Tracking Casual or Unrealistic Assumptions: 形式手法を使う時点でなにかしかの過程をおいているので注意
- Distributed Formal Verification in the Cloud: 検証問題を自動で分割して並行実行する手法はまだ十分に研究されていない
- Continous Formal Verification: システムのデプロイ前に最初のproofを見つけるのにかかる時間や労力は，その後proofをメンテする時間やコストと同等=1回使い切りでなく，継続的な利用が重要
- The Known Problems are Still Problems: AngularやLinuxといった巨大なシステムのセキュリティ検証は解決済みとは言えない，分散・並行システムの検証手法も未だにopen problem

Generating Formal Safety Assurances for High-Dimensional Reachability. (arXiv:2209.12336v3 [cs.RO] UPDATED)
https://ift.tt/eh7Go6J

Providing formal safety and performance guarantees for autonomous systems is becoming increasingly important. Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability analysis is a popular formal verification tool for providing these guarantees, since it can handle general nonlinear system dynamics, bounded adversarial system disturbances, and state and input constraints. However, it involves solving a PDE, whose computational and memory complexity scales exponentially with respect to the state dimensionality, making its direct use on large-scale systems intractable. A recently proposed method called DeepReach overcomes this challenge by leveraging a sinusoidal neural PDE solver for high-dimensional reachability problems, whose computational requirements scale with the complexity of the underlying reachable tube rather than the state space dimension. Unfortunately, neural networks can make errors and thus the computed solution may not be safe, which falls short of achieving our overarching goal to provide formal safety assurances. In this work, we propose a method to compute an error bound for the DeepReach solution. This error bound can then be used for reachable tube correction, resulting in a safe approximation of the true reachable tube. We also propose a scenario-based optimization approach to compute a probabilistic bound on this error correction for general nonlinear dynamical systems. We demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach in obtaining probabilistically safe reachable tubes for high-dimensional rocket-landing and multi-vehicle collision-avoidance problems.

Summary of our discussion:

Project Goal:

Utilize a large language model (LLM) to explore and potentially create a "class of classes" within a self-descriptive hierarchy using Coq.

Derive methods and descriptions for these classes through LLM prompts and feedback loops.

Key Points:

LLM Capabilities: Consider the limitations and strengths of the chosen LLM, especially in understanding type classes and formal languages like Coq.

Prompt Design: Provide clear, concise, and iterative prompts with relevant context (e.g., previous/next items, function purpose, evaluation criteria).

Feedback Loop: Establish clear criteria for evaluating generated functions and use the feedback to adapt prompts and guide the LLM.

Data Representation: Choose a consistent format for representing classes, methods, descriptions, and context for efficient processing.

Additional Considerations: 

Scaling for large hierarchies

Ethical implications of LLM bias

Human oversight and explainability

Computational resources

Potential Benefits:

Exploring relationships and insights within the hierarchy

Generating creative and diverse methods for different classes

Automating some aspects of method development

Challenges and Limitations:

LLMs might not always generate correct or functional Coq code.

The iterative process requires careful design and human intervention.

Scaling to large hierarchies might be computationally expensive.

Next Steps:

Define specific use cases and desired outcomes for the "class of classes" concept.

Choose a specific LLM and experiment with different prompt formats and feedback mechanisms.

Start with simple examples and gradually increase complexity as you gain confidence.

Monitor the LLM's performance and adapt your approach based on the results.

Additional Resources:

Coq libraries: CoqAssist, Coq extraction

Research on LLMs for code generation and formal verification

I hope this summary is helpful! Please let me know if you have any further questions or want to explore specific aspects in more detail.

# Implement Register Allocation Verifier
## Background
The register allocator is a critical component of our compiler infrastructure, ensuring efficient use of the limited register resources available on target architectures. To enhance confidence in its correctness and reliability, there's a need to verify that the register allocator operates as expected across a wide range of input programs.

## Objective
The goal is to develop a verifier for the register allocator that checks its correctness on arbitrary input programs. Although achieving a formal verification (proof of correctness for all possible programs) is not feasible, we aim to approach this level of assurance through statistical means. The verifier will assess the allocator's performance, highlighting any discrepancies or errors in its operation.

## Inspiration
Our approach draws inspiration from techniques described in Chris Fallin's blog post on Cranelift's instruction selection and register allocation [Cranelift: Fast Compilers for the Masses](https://cfallin.org/blog/2021/03/15/cranelift-isel-3/). This methodology provides a practical framework for implementing a similar verification tool within our project.

## Proposed Solution
- Verifier Design: The verifier will input generated programs, run them through the register allocator, and then validate the allocator's decisions. This process involves checking that the allocator has not only assigned registers efficiently but also preserved the semantic integrity of the original program.
- Statistical Validation: By employing a statistical approach, the verifier will analyze a broad set of generated programs, offering a high level of confidence in the allocator's overall correctness.
## Implementation Steps
1. Research and Analysis: Study the referenced approach used by Cranelift and other existing verification tools for register allocation.
2. Design Phase: Outline the architecture of the verifier, including its integration with the existing register allocator.
3. Program Generation: Implement or integrate a fuzzing engine capable of generating a wide variety of input programs for testing.
4. Semantic Equality Check: Develop a method for verifying that the semantics of a program remain unchanged post register allocation.
5. Testing and Iteration: Conduct extensive testing with the verifier, refining the approach based on findings.
## Potential Challenges
- Input Program Generation: Creating a robust and versatile fuzzing engine that can produce a comprehensive set of test cases poses a significant challenge.
- Semantic Equality Verification: Ensuring the semantic integrity of the program before and after register allocation requires sophisticated analysis tools, which are complex to develop and integrate.
- Performance Overheads: The verification process may introduce performance overheads, especially when analyzing large or complex input programs.
title: Implement register allocation verifier

This issue is related to #263, however I decided to re-raise it considering the original issue is just over 2 years old, and because there doesn't seem to have been any discussion on it. - Name: Lean 4 - Website: https://leanprover.github.io/ - Language Version: - Most recent release: v4.25.0-rc2 - Most recent stable releases: v4.24.0, v4.23.0 - Comments: From its documentation on Github (and also https://lean-lang.org/), Lean 4 is an open source proof assistant and programming language that is meant to enable maintainable and formally verified code. Its metaprogramming capabilities enable users to extend the language as necessary. --- - Test Frameworks: - For functional programming: [LTest](github.com/alexf91/LTest) is the only one I'm aware of (since there isn't a built-in test framework in Lean 4), although at the moment it doesn't seem to be very fleshed out.
However, if needed, I'm pretty sure I could throw together a fleshed out test framework from scratch by March of next year.

- For theorems: I'm sure a test framework wouldn't be needed in this case (considering there is none for Lean 3) - How to install: See [here](https://lean-lang.org/install/) for VSCode instructions, although installation should be possible through Atom using a similar method. - How to compile/run: Should be the same as or at least similar to Lean 3 (although I don't really know). - Any comments: Configuration dependencies for a project require either a `lakefile.lean` or `lakefile.toml` file (I've seen both). --- Closing notes: - On extensibility to more general programming challenges: I have been able to translate some of my own kata solutions to Lean 4 with somewhat similar (although slightly worse) performance overall, while also being able to verify that the data types needed to solve each problem are available natively. - Some of the (more notable) kata of which I have been able to translate my solution into Lean 4 include: - The Hashtag Generator (5 kyu) - Bitwise Sum (4 kyu) - Lowest base system (4 kyu) - BasE91 encoding & decoding (4 kyu) - The fusc function -- Part 2 (4 kyu) - Differentiate a polynomial (4 kyu)² - Memoized Log Cutting (4 kyu) - Sum Strings as Numbers (4 kyu)¹ - Matrix Determinant (4 kyu) - SKRZAT!!! (4 kyu)¹ - Rail Fence Cipher: Encoding and Decoding (3 kyu)² - Last digit of a huge number (3 kyu)¹ - Fabergé Easter Eggs crush test (3 kyu) - The Millionth Fibonacci Kata (3 kyu)¹ ³ - Power tower modulo n (2 kyu) - Faberge easter eggs crush test [linear] (1 kyu) - BECOME IMMORTAL (1 kyu) - The kata which I previously solved and am currently attempting to write a solution for in Lean 4: - Gould's Sequence (7 kyu) - 4 By 4 Skyscrapers (4 kyu) - Battleship Field Validator (3 kyu) - Fastest Code: Equal to 24 (2 kyu) - 6 By 6 Skyscrapers (2 kyu) - 7 By 7 Skyscrapers (1 kyu) - External Dependencies Requested: - [Mathlib4 (leanprover-community)](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/tree/master) - [Ctypes (alexf91)](https://github.com/alexf91/lean4-ctypes/tree/main/) --- ¹The Lean 4 translation can still be optimized, although not much more optimization should be needed to handle larger test cases.
²The Lean 4 translation needs to be more optimized before tagging with ¹.
³Translated using solutions I've used in the past, not the one used to solve the kata. :+1: reaction _might_ help to get this request prioritized.
